This source would indicate that there are psychiatric wards in at least ten general hospitals in these provinces. I believe these wards usually contain 20 to 40 beds.
Future development will depend on a number of factors, including the priority placed by the individual provinces on these services, which in turn will depend on continuing appraisal as to their relative value as compared to other aspects of the mental health program. subtopic: NEW BASIS FOR ASSESSMENT OF SUCCESSION DUTIES

speechtext:
On the order:
Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. C-37, an act respecting taxation of estates.-The Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NEW BASIS FOR ASSESSMENT OF SUCCESSION DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Senate has returned Bill No. C-37, an act respecting the taxation of estates, to the house with eight amendments. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that a situation in which there may be differences between the two houses is of a nature which has not arisen in the experience of parliament since 1947.
I may remind hon. members that the eight amendments are to be found in Votes and Proceedings of the house for Thursday, August 28, at pages 512 and 513. Of the eight amendments seven are perfectly acceptable so far as the government is concerned, and the

Estate Tax Act
tax purposes all parts of the income of the recipient of that superannuation or pension benefit equally, that is to say, is it going to be a pro rata calculation, or are we to assume that the income from the superannuation or pension benefit is either the bottom slice or the top slice of the recipient's income?
It is quite obvious that there is no guide whatever in this proposed amendment to indicate how the Department of National Revenue is to proceed in these matters. In this amendment there is simply nothing to define the basis upon which the calculation of assumed income tax is to be made. I am therefore obliged to say that this amendment, contriving as it purports to provide a new basis of calculation of capital value of these benefits, is quite unworkable. If it were enacted today one would simply not know how to go about putting it into effect.
In conclusion may I simply say that the problem of how most equitably to tax superannuation or pension payments in respect of their capital value at the date of death is a difficult matter. It is a matter which engaged our attention very fully before the bill was first introduced, and on it we received not only a large number of representations but I might say also the greatest variety of representations. There have been more representations on this subject in point of number than there has been agreement on the way in which this problem should be met, and we considered that in all the circumstances the most equitable way to proceed was to carry into the new bill the provisions of the present Dominion Succession Duty Act in this respect.
I may say that there is no finality to any tax legislation. Legislation of this kind must be constantly under review. I indicated in appearing before the banking and commerce committee of this house, as I did when I appeared before the banking and commerce committee of the Senate, that it is the government's intention to continue to bring under review this new legislation, when adopted, as well as other taxing legislation. There will always be differences of opinion as to the fairest and most equitable way in which to write the detailed provisions of taxing legislation. There is no finality to any such legislation. The Income Tax Act is a very good example. It was completely revised and codified in 1949, and every year since that time large numbers of amendments have been introduced.
While we believe that the present bill is a good bill and a major advance over the legislation in the present Dominion Succession Duty Act, I am quite prepared to say

that there is no such thing as a perfect taxation act, and it will be our intention to give continued study to any of these problems which have presented difficulty in connection with the language of the present bill. We are not keeping our minds closed on any of these subjects which have presented difficulties.
For the reasons that I have given, I submit to the house that the fourth amendment proposed by the Senate should not be accepted by the house. I therefore move, seconded by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness):
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this house agrees to the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. C-37, an act respecting the taxation of estates, with the exception of the fourth amendment to which this house disagrees for the following reasons:
1.	It creates discrimination in favour of a particular class of property.
2.	The amendment is unworkable.
3.	The amendment will reduce government revenues, and will particularly tend to reduce revenues from estates of larger value.
And that the Clerk of the house do carry the said message to the Senate.

subtopic: NEW BASIS FOR ASSESSMENT OF SUCCESSION DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister of Finance and the government have something of a fight on their hands with the other place, and I am not going to get into that fight. I think the other place is quite capable of standing up for its own views with respect to the points on which the minister differs with the amendment proposed.
On the other hand, I want to point out that the discussions in the banking and commerce committee of the other place were prolonged and thorough. Unlike our own banking and commerce committee, they did receive outside evidence. They received evidence from the chairman of the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, from the associate general counsel of the Sun Life Insurance Company, from a representative of the Montreal Trust Company, a representative of the trust association of Canada, and from two or three representatives who I thought should have been heard by our own banking and commerce committee-and I said so not only in the house but in the committee-Mrs. G. D. Finlayson, of the national council of women, Mrs. J. F. Flaherty of the Canadian Federation of university women.
I do not want the house to get the impression which it might get from hearing a radio commentary, such as I heard this morning, that the criticisms of the estates tax bill in the other place came entirely from supporters of the Liberal group in the Senate. When this bill was introduced in the Senate and debated on August 14, any criticisms

I made concerning the bill in this place were certainly greatly improved upon and exceeded by such newly appointed senators supporting the government as Senator Brunt and a former member of this house, Senator White. They had firm and strong criticism of the bill to make, and I do say that this amendment came to us after very careful consideration.
I do not intend to elaborate at any length with regard to the merits or demerits of the amendment in dispute. Already in the banking and commerce committee I have pointed out the hardship which results from the imposition of double taxation on both successions and pension income therefrom. I simply want to express a view which I think is generally highly endorsed, a view which has been expressed by the Canadian tax foundation and a view which was put forward during the sittings of our banking and commerce committee after an additional review had been made of the revised estates tax bill. The bulletin of the Canadian tax foundation had this to say on this subject in examining Bill No. C-37:
It also seems to us that something might finally have been done to alleviate the heavy burden of tax on pensions, annuities and other periodic payments that are subject to death duties and income tax almost simultaneously.
In criticising Bill No. 248, which was introduced in the previous session of parliament, the general view in all the briefs which I believe were received by the minister after the bill became public were well expressed in the brief of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, when they said this:
Comment is made here in our brief upon the whole question of the taxation of income rights, etc. This comment is made subsidiary to the general recommendation that pensions and death benefits be not subject to estate tax. Such rights are received over a term. It has always been undesirable that the tax on the capitalized value should be payable immediately when even the amount of tax itself may only be recovered by the recipient over a period or may never be recovered. In particular, it is invidious to assess and immediately collect tax based on a capitalized value, by the application of mortality tables, when the successor may not even live long enough to receive benefits equal to the assessed tax. It is excessively harsh that no account is taken of the impact of income tax when computing estate tax on such benefits and vice versa.
We do not propose, as I say, to make extensive comment on the conflict, if there is one, between the government and the Senate. I simply point out again that the criticisms in the other place were on a bi-partisan basis and that they reiterate and, I think, confirm criticisms which I myself and others advanced here when the bill was before us. I think those in our group will have to say
Estate Tax Act
"on division" with respect to the motion proposed by the minister.

subtopic: NEW BASIS FOR ASSESSMENT OF SUCCESSION DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the motion presented by the Minister of Finance should be supported not only on the ground of the main content of the motion, with which I am in complete and full agreement, but also to demonstrate, I would hope, as a result of its passing at this time that the House of Commons should be supreme in all matters affecting the revenues of this nation and the balance of ways and means.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River talked about the government having a fight on its hands. I doubt very much if that is really correct. I would assume that the members of the other place, in their good judgment, in their certain sense of security and wel-being, knowing full well the stature of the Canadian House of Commons in the minds of the public of this country, would have second thoughts and would very speedily agree to this motion which will pass this house today.
We in the C.C.F. will not be saying "on division", because we support the motion and are quite prepared to vote for it.
This is the first time in my memory in this house that the other place has amended a bill of the House of Commons in a way which would reduce the revenues to the national treasury. I would hope that such amendments would not be forthcoming from the other place in future much as I, in a given instance, might like to see certain revenues and certain taxes reduced. I feel that the other place has made not only a mistake in substance but a mistake as far as the operation of our Canadian parliament is concerned.
I do not for one moment question at this time the constitutional right of the other place to do such a thing, but I do not think it should be done. I do not imagine the government has a fight on its hands in the other place even though the government party does not command a majority there; but I would say that if the other place should reject this motion then there should be a conference, as is provided under our rules, between this chamber and the other place to consider appropriate amendments to the constitution of this country to make it abundantly clear that the Canadian House of Commons has the overriding authority.
I believe that hon. members of the other place perform a certain function in that they are able to look over legislation and make amendments, but I think the amendments they make should be considered more as suggestions than as amendments. If it appears necessary I believe there should be a working out of the final formula and method of

Estate Tax Act
procedure to make it abundantly clear that in main constitutional questions and money matters the Canadian House of Commons is supreme.
I agree with the purport of the argument of the Minister of Finance. The minister has a tremendous command of the English language, and he can make a very excellent case when he is on solid ground. I enjoyed listening to him present his case this morning. Listening to his extremely strong statements and well chosen phraseology I was pleased, for the first time in my memory, not to have them directed particularly at the opposition in this house. While the Minister of Finance seldom wins an argument in this house by way of unanimous vote, I am hoping that following the passage of this motion it will be made clear that the minister has spoken for the House of Commons and the Canadian people, and that the members of the other place will agree that that is the situation.
The Minister of Finance has demolished the substance of the amendment by pointing out that it is discriminatory and would work to the advantage of well to do persons receiving benefits from large estates, and that these exemptions that are already in the act provide a good measure of relief to a very small proportion of the population who under difficult circumstances are fortunate enough to have an interest in an estate of a value above $50,000. I accept the minister's statement because of his knowledge and the advice he is able to obtain from his officials that the suggested amendment would be unworkable. It is perfectly clear that if it were to pass it would result in a reduction of revenue to the national treasury. Believing that revenues in this case on the basis of the merit of the amendment alone should not be reduced, and also on the principle that the House of Commons should be supreme in this matter, I shall certainly be very pleased to support the motion.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have one further comment to correct any possible wrong impression that may have been left by the remarks of my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. He may have left the impression in the minds of some that this bill is going to create a severe hardship in the matter of the rate of payment or what is sometimes called the periodicity of payment of taxes with respect to those periodical payments in the form of superannuation or pension benefits. Where these benefits flow through the executor of the estate the estate tax thereon is a charge on the estate and not, under this bill, on the successor, the recipient of the superannuation or pension benefit.
That is the first point. I wish to make it perfectly clear that if payments of this kind flow through the executor, then no estate tax liability except in a secondary sense is laid upon the recipient of the superannuation or pension benefit.
In the other case, where the payment flows not through the executor but goes direct to the successor, the recipient of the pension or superannuation payment, provision is made in clause 15 of this bill for payment of the liability in six annual instalments. speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-51, to amend the Customs Act.
He said: In his budget speech my colleague the Minister of Finance announced that I would shortly submit a bill to parliament to amend the valuation provisions of the Customs Act. The present law is adequate to deal with most cases of dumping or distress selling, but does not provide a safeguard against sales at prices below cost-plus. It appears to us necessary to rectify this

situation in order to protect the Canadian economy against unfair competition and the virtual importation of unemployment as a result of goods being brought in at prices which are below the cost of production plus a reasonable addition for selling cost, administrative cost and profit. This, then is the primary reason for revising the present law.
Experience over the years with the current valuation provisions of the Customs Act has indicated a want of certainty as to the true meaning of certain phrases and indeed sections, bringing about resultant difficulty not only for departmental administration but also placing an undue burden on both the tariff board and the exchequer court. Developments have been such as to point up the desirability of clarifying and rendering beyond question the meaning of the provisions which have been giving difficulty. It seems prudent, therefore, to take this opportunity, when the valuation sections are being amended, to resolve this problem and at the same time to regroup the various sections in more appropriate order.
In this regard, the proposed wording of the bill does not contemplate any material departure from current practice. The cardinal principle of valuation which has been in effect since confederation and which is to continue to apply is based upon the fair market value of like goods when sold in the home market in similar circumstances. A number of subsidiary and clarifying rules have been laid down with a view to establishing a more workable procedure for determining value for duty.
In his budget speech my colleague the Minister of Finance also stated that I would submit a bill to amend the Customs Act in the matter of appeals from our decisions under item 1201 of the Customs Tariff Act. This item is the one which prohibits the importation of material of a treasonable, seditious, immoral or indecent character. In a recent judgment the tariff board questioned whether it is the appropriate body to hear such appeals. The government shares this doubt, and accordingly provision is being made in the new bill which is before us today for appeal in such cases to be made to the courts.
Section 45 of the Customs Act deals with appeals to the exchequer court from decisions of the tariff board. At this time the opportunity is being taken to revise and clarify the procedure, which should make for a more orderly disposition of cases coming before this body. Three main changes are involved as follows:
(a)	The appeal period has been increased from 30 days to 60 days.

(b)	The necessity for the appellant and the deputy minister to obtain leave to appeal has been eliminated, but persons who entered an appearance at the tariff board must still obtain such leave.
(c)	A complete code of appeal procedure, including right of cross appeal.
Those, Mr. Speaker, include the salient points which are embodied in the bill now before the house. Later on in the day, when the debate is completed, I will have an opportunity to deal with any arguments which might be raised for or against the bill and also, of course, in committee to clarify any matters in respect of the various sections.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister in introducing this bill took five minutes to deal with one of the most important customs measures introduced into this house in many years, a bill which could have a far-reaching and harmful effect on our trade and, indeed, on Canada's trading relationships. He took five minutes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext: An example of the beauty of brevity.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
That was a quarter of the time which was required in this house this morning for an unnecessary division, and that is all we are being given by way of explanation of the bill and analysis of its contents, which as I have said is of very far-reaching importance. Indeed it is probably as important as any customs bill which has been introduced into this house for many, ma'ny years. The minister has said, of course, that this bill is really confined-and I believe these are the words he used-largely to subsidiary and clarifying rules. I hope, however, to demonstrate that it is far more than that and I regret, though perhaps not as much as I would have regretted half an hour ago, that I shall have to take a certain amount of time to give the views of our party on this matter.
The bill before us deals with the problem of the determination of the value of imported goods for duty purposes. It is a subject which is as complex as it is important because, as hon. members know, a valuation for duty purposes can be as important as the duty itself. It is because of this importance that it is necessary for an objective and sound basis to be established for the determination of value. The necessity for that is obvious.
It seems to me that three requirements should be met in establishing this basis. Firstly there is the necessity of preserving the rights of parliament over taxation because, as we know, a duty is a tax and a valuation can be a duty. If parliament

Customs Act
determines a rate but the valuation is left to a minister or his officials, or both, then parliament's rights over this form of tax are reduced accordingly and may be nullified by administrative action.
Second, there is the requirement to prevent unfair discrimination between those who, as consumers and taxpayers, are bearing the tariff burden, unfair discrimination which could result from arbitrary valuations through administrative action. Finally there is the requirement to create and maintain orderly conditions for international trade. I believe it would be quite impossible to meet that requirement if nations customarily used arbitrary valuations for customs purposes, that this would stop trade expansion and would introduce rigidities and restrictions into trade.
To meet these three requirements, as I have said, an objective and equitable basis of valuation for duty purposes must be established. I realize, of course, that such a basis applicable to every case which might arise is very difficult to find indeed, and I suppose it is impossible; but a fair basis for general application must be found and must be embodied in our law. If an alternative is required it should be used only if the primary basis cannot be applied; should be used only in special cases. That principle has been recognized in the present customs law.
I agree with the minister that the basis which we have established in this country over the years is fair market value, though I am not sure it will remain fair market value if this bill becomes law. Fair market value in accord with prices in the country of origin is the best and fairest basis obtainable. This we have found in the light of experience. This principle is included in GATT and is generally accepted by the members of GATT. I admit, of course, that there are other bases included in GATT and, indeed, in our law, but they are for use only when fair market value cannot be applied.
I know, as the minister knows, that arbitrary valuations are permitted under article 19 of GATT. This is, of course, an escape clause, I agree. We have, however, more than once protested, and vigorously protested, when that article has been used in a way contrary to the spirit and objectives of GATT. We have always taken the position in our negotiations under GATT that this article should be restricted to real emergencies and used only as a last resort. If it is not if it is used in some other way, then it invites retaliation which can destroy GATT, can restrict trade and can even hurt the country which is applying the other form of valuation.
The present Canadian law on this matter is designed to meet the three requirements I

have mentioned. It is in conformity with the spirit and the objectives of GATT except possibly for one section of the present law, namely section 38, to which I shall return later. Incidentally that particular section, No. 38, was put in by the Conservative government of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. It was, I admit, retained by Liberal governments after 1935 to be available in a genuine emergency. But the fact that the Liberal government had that and only that in mind in retaining this particular clause is shown by the fact that in the 22 years of Liberal administration that clause was used only once and then, perhaps ironically, after the general election of June 19, 1957. The only time that clause was used was, I believe, in connection with the importation of strawberries.
The new bill, however, changes all this. It alters drastically, and not in a subsidiary or unimportant way as the minister indicated, the present system of valuation. I hope I will be able to convince the minister of that before I finish.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext: It will take a lot of speeches to do that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
You have no idea how long this is going to be.
It embodies a new and wrong approach. Furthermore, the government must intend to use these new powers which it is requesting, else what whould be the purpose of making these changes? I suggest that if this bill becomes law, fair market value is likely to become an exception rather than the rule. Therefore this bill in its provisions prejudices that objective basis which I have mentioned and it widens, I think in a dangerous way, the application of arbitrary valuations. It does that first of all through a greater use of the cost of production test-and I will have something to say about that test later

and second, through wider discretionary powers given to the minister, to the governor in council and to officials.
How then is this principle on which we have based our law for so many years, this principle of fair market value, to be restricted in this bill? It is to be restricted in at least three ways. I intend to deal with this matter now only in a general way because this is the second reading stage, but when we come to the committee stage we on this side will deal with each clause as it arises, and I think we can show how these clauses will restrict the fair market value principle. If hon. members will look at clause 39 of the bill, for example-I single this out as one glaring illustration-they will find that it reads:
Where the minister is satisfied that material injury has been or may be caused to any industry-

I draw those words to the attention of the house-"has been or may be caused"-
-in Canada or any portion thereof, by reason of the importation of any new or unused goods or class of such goods at a value for duty less than the cost of production thereof, plus a reasonable amount for gross profit, he may so report to the governor in council, and, notwithstanding anything in this act, the governor in council may order that the value for duty of those goods or that class of goods shall be increased to an amount equal to the cost of production thereof plus a reasonable amount for gross profit, having regard to the gross profit generally earned in that trade in the country of export, to be determined in the manner prescribed in section 37.
This means that in all cases, not only where injury has been caused but where injury may be caused, the minister and the cabinet will have full discretionary powers to determine the value for duty purposes.
Then there is clause 38, subclauses (b) (c) and (d) which I will not quote, but in which provision is laid down-and we will come back to this in detail during the committee stage-that the value for duty shall be determined in such a manner as the minister prescribed. And in these cases, fair market value even when it can be determined will not be used. In my opinion those clauses, or certainly part of them, are contrary to our obligations under GATT. They give the minister far-reaching discretionary and arbitrary powers to use.
There is another clause, clause 37, which again I will not quote, but I will come back to it later. It states that when comparison for duty has to be made with similar goods the value for duty, unlike the provision in the present legislation, is determined by cost of production plus gross profit. Again, fair market value is abandoned. Clause 36 also contains some new conditions which must be met before the fair market value rule can be applied, just as clauses 37, 38, 39 and 40 lay down some new limitations on that rule.
To sum up, the cardinal principle for determining value for duty which has been used in this country for so long, that is to say the fair market value of like or similar goods sold in the home market in similar circumstances, is being so greatly weakened in this bill as to become almost valueless. It will become, as I have said, the exception rather than the rule as the government uses the new provisions. It is being replaced by cost of production plus gross profit or reasonable profit, or by the discretionary and arbitrary power of the minister to fix valuation.
The cost of production test is an impracticable basis for valuation, often an impossible basis; therefore we are left with arbitrary valuation. I say, therefore, that because of this development and because of what is 57071-3-2831
Customs Act
implicit and explicit in this bill, parliament's right to tax and to control taxes is being prejudiced and weakened. It puts the executive in control. It increases the dangers of discrimination as between taxpayers, and it ignores both the spirit and the objectives of GATT. In consequence we oppose this bill, and we oppose it strongly. We will do our utmost to defeat it and we will do our best, if we cannot defeat it, to amend it and to make it at least a better bill.
This is important because so much now will depend on the administration of this measure, and because that is so it is important to ascertain its purposes, in so far as we are able to do so, in the eyes of the government as well as to trace, as I propose to do, the legislative history of these provisions.
The Minister of Finance in his budget speech indicated that these provisions which are before us now were designed to protect Canadian producers against dumping. This party and the governments of this party have always supported, and we still support, legitimate anti-dumping measures. Our record in this connection when we were in power is shown by the inclusion in the Customs Tariff Act of the anti-dumping provision in section 6; it is shown by the inclusion in the present Customs Act of sections 38(1) and 35(12). It is shown in the bill we passed in 1950 dealing with seasonal rates of specific duties.
So we are not opposed to anti-dumping legislation. We have supported it in the past and we have enacted it in the past. But we are opposed to extending the power of the executive in this way in the guise of adding to anti-dumping legislation. The Minister of Finance-and I quote from page 1247 of Hansard of this session-had this to say:
The government intends to defend Canadian producers against the practice of dumping, whatever form it may take. This will require the strengthening of the present valuation provisions of the Customs Act and their effective enforcement. To this end my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) will shortly submit a bill to parliament amending the valuation provisions of the Customs Act-
This is the bill now before us. I continue:
-to add a provision to section 35 along the lines of the legislation in effect prior to 1948-
I will show what that means later. I continue:
-requiring that, where appropriate, the value for duty of imported goods shall not be less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit.
The Minister of National Revenue who has introduced this bill made a statement in this house on July 3, and repeated it this morning, in which he related the problem of unemployment to this bill. On that date he

Customs Act
said that the amendments which are now before us would help to deal with the unemployment situation by dealing with goods brought into this country at below cost of production. As reported at page 1892 of Hansard at that date the Minister of National Revenue said:
After all, the term "fair market value" must surely have some meaning, and it must be remembered that it has been determined time and time again that the market value has really had no reference whatsoever to fair market value, and that anyone by making a few sales in the country of origin could then send the goods here, avoiding dumping duty. And when such goods are sold superficially below cost they threaten not only Canadian industry but, what is more important, the employees of Canadian industry.
With the objective of that statement, the protection of Canadian industry against unfair competition brought about by dumping as it was understood in the past, we of course have no quarrel. In fact we support it. But we do question the minister's view that you can curb unemployment in this country by trying to export it. Some of us will remember very well that this was the remedy adopted by Mr. Bennett and his government from 1930 to 1935. From what the minister has said it is clear that the government attaches importance to these amendments not only as an instrument of protection but as a cure for unemployment. I venture to state the results in that respect will not be good, and the experience of the period 1930 to 1935 to which I have already alluded strengthens these doubts in my mind.
Perhaps I should now make a short historical review which will help to explain why we have such strong doubts about the wisdom and value of these amendments. In making this review, of course, we must keep in mind a clear distinction between the dumping provisions in the Customs Tariff Act and the valuation provisions as they exist in the present amendments to the Customs Act.
The anti-dumping provisions of the Customs Tariff Act are in section 6 of that act, and I believe were first introduced in this country in 1904. Those provisions in the present act over the years became the standard for other countries who adopted them, and indeed they became the standard for GATT where they are embodied, I believe in articles 6 and 7. The word "dumping" is defined in the Customs Tariff Act in these words:
-sale In Canada of goods at a price lower than the fair market value in the principal markets of the exporting country.
When dumping was proven under those provisions a duty was charged on the higher price and a penalty of not more than 15 per

cent was imposed. These provisions, we should remember, are not affected by the present amendments which deal with valuations for duty under the Customs Act.
Let us look at the valuation provisions of the present Customs Act. Subsection 2 of section 35 of the Customs Act is the present basic valuation provision. It reads:
The value for duty shall be the fair market value, at the time when and place from which the goods were shipped to Canada, of like goods when sold in like quantities for home consumption in the ordinary course of trade under fully competitive conditions and under comparable conditions of sale.
That concept of fair market value-and the house will pardon me if I go back a little in Canadian history-goes back as far as the Galt tariff of 1859. It continued unchanged and indeed was adopted by other countries, which is a tribute to its wisdom and value, until 1921 when the Conservative government of that year amended the Customs Act to introduce a new principle; cost of production plus reasonable profit, as the value for duty. I believe that was the first time that principle was introduced into our customs legislation, and it was done under Mr. Meighen's government. It did not last very long and was repealed the next year by the Liberal government which came into power in 1922.
The reasons for that action are set out very clearly in the House of Commons debates of that time, when Mr. Fielding said this was an attempt to boost the tariff without letting the people of Canada know what was being done by creating a fictitious price in order that the government might increase the duty. He argued that cheapness of itself was no reason for keeping out goods, and should be distinguished from dumping. That clause was repealed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before one o'clock in developing my arguments against the provisions of this bill I had shown that in 1921 the Conservative government introduced the principle of cost of production into valuation for duty; that their act in this regard was repealed by the Liberal government in 1922, and that this cost of production formula did not reappear until the

government of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett came into power in 1930, when it was used as a formula to combat unemployment by increasing protection.
This Bennett formula, if I may call it that, provided that the value for duty of new and unused goods in no case was to be less than the cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada plus reasonable advances for selling costs and profit, that the minister should be the sole judge of what constituted a reasonable advance in the circumstances and that his decision thereon was to be final. The leader of the opposition of that day strongly opposed those provisions as we are opposing the provisions of this bill today. The leader of the opposition at that time, Mr. Mackenzie King, stated as reported in Hansard for 1930 at page 213, and I repeat it today in connection with this bill-
The government proposes ... to take power to fix an arbitrary valuation for customs purposes on whatever articles it likes, and to continue it as long as it likes.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the same criticism could be levelled against this legislation as an open invitation to arbitrary valuations and to administrative protection. In 1930 Mr. Mackenzie King argued, as I am attempting to argue today, that the power to impose a duty is the power to tax; that this power belongs to the Commons and should not be parted with or delegated to any government whatever, except in a strictly limited way for a genuine emergency. The then leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackenzie King, said at that time:
The bill

He was referring to the 1930 bill.
-is wholly subversive of responsible government in every sense of the word and should not for one moment be countenanced.
We take the same position in regard to the bill before us. Mr. Ralston, a leading member of the opposition at that time, continued the attack and objected because the tariff-making authority was being shifted from parliament to the executive. This is one of the main bases for our objection to this bill. He argued, and the argument can be used against this bill-
It is simply an enactment for the purpose of providing that the government without any cheek or control by parliament may make tariffs to suit the situation or to suit their own particular tariff ideas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal warnings at that time, warnings of the effect of this kind of legislation on our economy went unheeded, but they were later proven to be right, and they have since, I think, been fully vindicated in the attitude they took at that time. It is
Customs Act
the attitude we are taking today in regard to this bill. A recognized Canadian authority on customs matters who is now a member of the tariff board, Professor Elliott, had this to say in his book "Tariff Procedures and Trade Barriers", at page 187, talking about the provisions of the Bennett legislation:
This set of administrative provisions was Canada's distinctive contribution to the trade barriers of the great depression.
Later on he said:
That Canada's methods were effective in obstructing trade is attested by the complaints of British and foreign exporters and of Canadian importers; by the reports of a Canadian royal commission and of the United States tariff commission; by the pains taken to obtain concessions for empire goods at the Ottawa conference and by the fact that the govern-men was able to pacify Canadian manufacturers while making concessions; by the United States' threat to exclude Canada from the benefits of the earlier treaties under the trade agreements act; and finally by the provisions of Canada's trade agreements with the United States in 1935 and 1938.
This is what Mr. Elliott had to say. Another Canadian customs authority, Professor Blake of Winnipeg, in his study of Canadian customs administration reached similar conclusions when he said in regard to this earlier legislation:
An enormous increase in the power of the Minister of National Revenue over the tariff, and a concomitant decline in the power of parliament, resulted from the legislation of 1930.
Later on he said:
It was decided to place the tariff weapon in the hands of the "war cabinet", and this was accomplished, neatly and effectively, through the Customs Act. By a process of extending, amending, and increasing the Canadian executive presented to the world a customs barrier which in many of its aspects resembled the crudest form of mercantilism.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that again we in this house in 1958 are being asked to go back to 1930 in the amendments to the bill before us, amendments which are in the view of the minister merely clarifications but which, as I have said, in our view go very much beyond that. The fact is that the cost of production as a basis for customs evaluation is an arbitrary and subjective valuation test. What is it? The cost of production in Canada or the cost of production in the country of export? How is it to be ascertained? Which of many differing costs is to be used, and what is reasonable profit? Why, the minister who introduced this bill is himself on record already in this session as to how arbitrary in his opinion is the concept of cost of production. At page 1803 of Hansard of July 1 the minister had this to say; we were talking about coal:
They talked about producing coal at cost and using it for producing power. As the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond said, "What is cost?" It could be anything.

Customs Act
The minister told us on July I that the cost of production could be anything. We say that under this legislation it can be anything the cabinet arbitrarily decides it to be, that in doing so they establish the value for duty, and that is the power to make and increase tariffs at the will of the executive.
But we cannot leave the problem at that point. In the discussion of this very matter in 1930 the minister of national revenue of that time, Mr. Ryckman, left no other conclusion in the minds of members of the house of that day but that the cost of production he had in mind was the cost of production in Canada. He stated at that time that he could quite conceive, as can everyone else, that goods might be sold in Canada at below the cost of production in Canada, and that this might be what he would call unfair or piratical trade. At another point in the debate of 1930, as found at page 288 of Hansard of September 16, the minister of national revenue of that day said:
If goods manufactured in another country were sold continually in Canada at a price lower than they can be produced here our manufacturers would be driven out of business.
So, Mr. Speaker, we wonder whether the present Minister of National Revenue subscribes to the point of view held on this matter by his predecessor who had the misfortune to introduce similar legislation almost three decades ago. On this particular point Mr. Ralston was quick to point out, as I should like to point out now, that the philosophy proposed at that time by the minister of national revenue would endanger the whole basis of international exchange of goods. Mr. Ralston said then, and I believe he was right, as found at page 289 of Hansard of September 16, 1930:
Canadians are selling many of our exports at a price below the cost of production in the country where those goods are sold. That is the reason we are selling them there. We are not building a barbwired fence around Canada and swapping jack-knives with ourselves. We are selling all over the world.
That is something we have to keep in mind in this country as we discuss customs matters. The use of this test of cost of production as a method of valuation has led us into difficulties in the past and we fear it will do so again. The historic position of the Liberal party is opposed to it. Liberal spokesmen, as we have seen, pointed out its dangers in 1921. In 1922 the Liberal government repealed a provision based on this test. The Liberal party fought it again in 1930 and, as soon as it came into office in 1935, the arbitrary valuations were removed through trade agreements with the United States and then the arbitrary valuation provision was repealed in 1948.

That point perhaps requires further elaboration in view of the statement of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. The Minister of Finance has already pointed out, and quite correctly, that the cost of production provision as a basis for valuation was not repealed by a Liberal government until 1948. But he did not go further and point out that this cost of production feature of our tariff law had declined in importance and that its use had been restricted by trade agreements made by the Mackenzie King government after 1935 until it had become virtually inoperative. True, its formal repeal was not made until 1948, when it was formally done in order to reconcile our law with the requirements of the general agreements on tariffs and trade. But steps had been taken long before 1948 to render its provisions, as I have said, virtually inoperative.
The trade agreement between Canada and the United States at that time, 1935, involved an exchange of notes relating to this very point. In that agreement both governments gave undertakings that the fair market value should be taken for duty purposes. That was the first step to do away with this iniquitous cost of production test and arbitrary valuation feature of the Bennett legislation. The Liberal government removed about half the arbitrary values on United States goods on January 1, 1936.

speechtext:
Yes, that was when removal took place; and the remaining dumping valuations on United States goods were removed in the second United States-Canada trade agreement in 1938. Similar action was taken in all the other trade agreements we signed during that period when our trade was again on the upgrade. But, as I have just said, this particular provision in the legislation was not formally removed until it was rescinded in 1948, although it had been virtually inoperative for many years before that.
Surely it should now be clear, Mr. Speaker, to all hon. members that this particular technique about which I have been talking has been a favoured and exclusive instrument of commercial policy used by Conservative governments. It is now being reintroduced with its background of failure and its association with the depression period of Conservative rule from 1930 to 1935.
At this stage I am not going to make a detailed examination of the provisions of the bill, but I wish merely to use one illustration to show the kind of arbitrary powers the government would have if the bill were approved by parliament. Let us suppose for the sake of argument, and perhaps it is a realistic argument, that it is felt desirable to

give more protection by executive action outside parliament to the Canadian primary textile industry against United States competition. If the government decided to do that it could choose from three courses of action which are permitted under three different sections of the bill.
In the first place, under new section 40A (7) (c), if the governor in council, the cabinet, is satisfied that United States textiles "are being imported into Canada under such conditions as to prejudicially or injuriously affect the interests of Canadian producers or manufacturers, the governor in council may authorize the minister to determine the value for duty"-

(b) the goods imported.. .are intended to be... further manufactured in Canada or are intended to enter into the course of manufacture in Canada... the value for duty shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes.

In fact, it is true to say that the powers given the minister under section 38 are even wider than those given to the governor in council to deal with similar cases under section 39 or section 40A (7) (c).
Then there is one other point I want to mention, namely the effect of this legislation on the British preferential tariff. This is certainly a point which deserves to be raised at this stage, because it has a direct relationship to our imports from the United Kingdom. Under section 38 of the old legislation, which under the proposed bill, with one change, becomes section 40A (7) (c), it will be noted that the so-called anti-dumping valuation cannot be used for goods "entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff". Yes. Section 38 of the present act, which I think is clause 40A (7) (c) of the bill we are now considering. The government in this new bill, in its amendments, are maintaining that provision giving British goods exceptional treatment. They are maintaining that provision, but it now has no real significance of any kind because it is probably not its intention to use that provision very much since there are other provisions in this bill which give the government full power without such a qualification. I refer to the new section 39 under which-and this is an important change, which according to the government is to be a safeguard against dumping -goods entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff are not exempted.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is another blow at British exports to this country just a few weeks before the commonwealth economic conference. But that is not the worst thing. From now on, under section 38 the value for duty of all British goods which are not fully manufactured products will be determined in a manner prescribed by the minister, so the government will be in a position to discriminate against such British goods as woollen textiles, whether or not dumping practices have been used. That is under section 38 of the new bill.
In s*.:ort, Mr. Speaker, this is bad and dangerous legislation, especially when it is viewed in the light of economic history. It requires parliament to surrender many of its rights in this most important field of taxation. It gives

Customs Act
wide and arbitrary powers to the minister and the governor in council. It threatens the best interests of Canadians consumers, importers and exporters who are already bearing a heavy burden imposed by our tariffs. It will be a hard blow to GATT, and it can expose our country to damaging retaliation by other nations.
We do not know, of course, Mr. Speaker, the intentions of the government in applying these regulations. We do not know what are the industrial sectors that the government intends to protect with these wide and arbitrary powers. We do know, however, that once it has yielded to pressures in one sector, it will be extremely difficult not to do the same for others. We do know also that the first industrial sector would likely be that of primary textiles, according to previous statements made by members of the government.
Hence in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say a word about this particular problem. We all know that our primary textile industry in this country has been going through great difficulties for a long period of time. We know that in fact it has enjoyed real prosperity only when Canadian demand was abnormally high and foreign producers were not in a position to take advantage of our market.
I am not going to attempt at this stage, Mr. Speaker, to analyse the sources of weakness of this most important Canadian industry in terms of production and employment. Most of the causes of these difficulties have been indicated in two special studies which were prepared for and under the auspices of the Gordon commission. One is entitled "The Canadian Primary Textiles Industry" and the other "Canadian Secondary Manufacturing Industry". The reports of the tariff board are also interesting in this respect.
I want to emphasize, however, that these difficulties which are being experienced, and which have been experienced now for many years, are not due to the lack of Canadian skill or efficiency in this field or to the prevailing wages in this industry in comparison with the over-all level of wages in Canada. The causes are much deeper and more basic. For instance, the size of the domestic market, the great variety of tastes of Canadian consumers who are influenced, of course, by United States fashions; the lack of specialization within our own industry and technological changes are some of the factors that have brought about the present difficult situation.
I myself am convinced that some form of government assistance and encouragement will be needed in order to maintain this important Canadian industry and increase its

productivity. But we on this side of the house do not feel that government assistance of this kind should take the exclusive form of ever-greater protection against foreign competition, because such a remedy does very little indeed to cure the industry of its basic difficulties.
I obviously cannot outline now what are the other forms of government assistance that might be adopted, but I hope to have, before long, an occasion to do so. I firmly believe, however-and I want to emphasize this-that if the government feels at present that the industry needs more protection, it should have the courage to follow the only normal democratic method and ask parliament to increase the tariff either against ordinary foreign competition or against dumping, rather than trying with this bill in effect to by-pass parliament, to ask for wide and discretionary powers and impose arbitrary values. That is not the way to do it, Mr. Speaker. This approach, in our view, is the wrong one not only from the point of view of our democratic and parliamentary institutions but also from the point of view of our best long term economic interests in promoting orderly commercial relationships.
The bill now before us purports to protect Canadian industry against dumping and, as I said before lunch, with that purpose we are in agreement. Our good faith in that respect is shown by the measures introduced by Liberal governments in the past to give Canadian industry bona fide protection against illegitimate dumping, but this bill goes much further than that. It is a restrictive measure, as we see it, and puts restrictions on trade expansion; indeed, it is obstructive of the expansion of trade. In addition it gives unnecessarily arbitrary powers to the minister and the cabinet which entrench on the rights of parliament in this most important aspect of taxation policy.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith): That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
That this bill be not now read a second time because of new provisions for arbitrary valuations which transfer the tariff-making authority from parliament to the minister and the cabinet, contrary to the principles of responsible government and the essential right of parliament to tax."

Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. feel that this matter should not be proceeded with at this time. There are a great many reasons why we feel it is a mistake, and we will endeavour to put those reasons on record.
Canada, perhaps more than any other nation in the world, is dependent for a prosperous economy on the continuance of large scale trade and an expansion of trade, and I think perhaps more than any other nation we should be most careful to do nothing which would impede trade and prevent its expansion. I have in my hand Trade of Canada showing exports for December 1957, and I see that our exports in 1957 amounted to the very large total of $4,840 million. Anything that is likely to result in the reduction of our exports because we set up barriers to trade should not be lightly entered upon. Many of our main industries depend very greatly for their prosperity on a large export market.
In 1957 the value of agricultural and vegetable products going into export amounted to $831 million; animals and animal products, $302 million; fibrous textiles and textile products, $27 million; wood, wood products and paper, $1,456 million; iron and its products, $520 million; non-ferrous metals and their products, $1,006 million; chemicals and allied products, $195 million, and other miscellaneous commodities $154 million.
Canada was for many years the third exporting nation of the world, but according to information given to the Gordon commission and contained in the report, The Future of Canada's Export Trade, by 1955 Canada had dropped to fifth position, behind the United States, the United Kingdom, the Federal Republic of Germany and France. I submit that it would not be in the interests of our economy to take any steps which might result in a reduction of our exports and a general reduction in our trade.
Thus we have to look at this bill most carefully, and we find in it certain principles

to which we object. We object to the principle of the valuation of imports into this country on the basis of an arbitrary cost of production to which is added an arbitrary gross profit. We object to this bill because the decisions that will be taken will be decisions flowing from the cabinet or from the minister. How often in the past have we heard the Prime Minister object to government by order in council, government by cabinet decision? Hansard contains innumerable such references by the Prime Minister. And if there was one thing which beyond any other factor resulted in the Conservative party obtaining office, I believe it was that they were able to sell this principle to the Canadian public; that parliament should be supreme, that the supremacy of parliament should always be maintained, and that the governor in council should not be given authority to set in an arbitrary way such things as tariffs.
Under this legislation the governor in council will in certain circumstances arbitrarily establish a cost of production plus gross profit price with regard to goods entering into this country and for the purpose of establishing tariffs. This government is apparently going to acquire much more detailed information about the cost of production in foreign countries than it has been able to obtain regarding the cost of production at home. We have on the statute books the Agricultural Stabilization Act, in which the government has agreed to set certain floor prices for Canadian agricultural products based on the cost of production.
When we have asked whether these statistics on the cost of production of important agricultural commodities are available we have been informed that they are not. When farm organizations have come to Ottawa and asked that these figures be produced they have been informed that they are not obtainable because it has been impossible to ascertain the cost of producing these agricultural commodities. If that is the case, how much more impossible will it be for Canada to decide on the cost of production of goods coming into this country from foreign countries?
Another reason we feel this bill is not well timed is that it is being proceeded with just a few weeks before the forthcoming commonwealth conference. How can we reasonably expect an expansion of trade with commonwealth countries, and how can we reasonably expect the conference to succeed, if two weeks before the conference takes place parliament by passing this measure increases trade barriers against goods coming into this country from the commonwealth?
Customs Act
As has already been pointed out, section 38, subsection 1 of the existing Customs Act now provides for certain arbitrary powers, as follows:
38. (1) Where at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the governor in council on a report from the minister that goods of any kind not entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff or any lower tariff are being imported into Canada either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers or manufacturers, the governor in council may authorize the minister to fix the value for duty of any class or kind of such goods, and notwithstanding any other provision of this act, the value so fixed shall be deemed to be the fair market value of such goods.
Here is an arbitrary fixing of values, but it is an arbitrary fixing of values limited to those goods not entitled to enter under the British preferential tariff. This new bill removes this section and by section 39 allows the same arbitrary valuation of all goods coming into this country, no matter from what nation. One of the most significant purposes of this bill is to make it possible for the governor in council to erect further barriers based on arbitrary valuation against goods coming into this nation from commonwealth countries. We feel that the principle of this bill is wrong, and we believe most strongly that it should not be invoked against British goods by removing this exemption.
There has been a long history in this country of enactment of legislation such as we have before us today. In spite of the very learned statement by the Leader of the Opposition and the many excellent facts he brought forth, it has not always been the Conservative party which took the initiative in this direction. The record of the Liberal party is not without blemish. In 1922 under the prime minister of that day, Mr. Mackenzie King, the following amendment was placed on the statute books of this country. Section 3 of chapter 18 of the 1922 statutes reads as follows:
3. The said Customs Act is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 47 thereof:
"47. (a) If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the governor in council on a report from the minister of customs and excise, that natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada, either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers, the governor in council may, in any case or class of cases, authorize the minister to value such goods for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of this act, and the value so determined shall be held to be the fair market value thereof.
The same kind of arbitrary valuation about which the Leader of the Opposition complained so effectively this afternoon is found in the statutes of this country in 1922, placed there by a Liberal government. But

in those days the tables were completely turned; the situation was not that which we find in parliament today. At that time we had as leader of the opposition the Right Hon. Positive steps should be taken to assure adequate and continuous operation of canning and processing facilities.
Further we would suggest that an annual federal-provincial agricultural conference, attended by representatives of the federal and provincial governments, producers organizations, producers marketing and sales agencies and processors, for the purpose of orderly marketing and processing of fruit and vegetable products, should be arranged. We feel that this is an important provision. We would suggest the encouragement of international co-operation between Canadian grower organizations and United States grower organizations to undertake negotiations and discussions for the orderly marketing, on an agreed basis, of fruit and vegetable products between our two countries. We understand that to a degree such co-operative policies are already in effect. They provide at certain times of the year for the orderly importation into Canada of certain fruits from the United States and conversely orderly export of certain Canadian fruits during certain other parts of the year into the United States.
We feel that the provisions which this bill contains should not be proceeded with, and particularly not proceeded with at this time, in the light of the coming commonwealth trade conference. Canada, as one of the major trading nations of the world, is in no position to start down the road that leads to increased trade barriers and a worsening of our trade position.
We feel that there is another reason why we should not embark on such a policy at this time and that is the growing threat in the field of international trade as a result of the current Soviet economic trade offensive. It is not wise for Canada, it is not wise for other countries of the western world to undertake measures which will make trade

Customs Act
more difficult at a time when the Soviet union and the countries associated with it have embarked on a very aggressive program of expansion of international trade. We feel, Mr. Speaker, that the problems which this measure endeavours to deal with should be dealt with in other ways.
In introducing the measure the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) said that he thought it would help employment in our country. I am very fearful that any such measure which can result in increased trade barriers will have the very opposite effect and that it will result in more unemployment and further difficulties for the major export industries of our country which are so important to our economy and to which our nation owes so much. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, at this stage, enter the debate on the bill introduced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan)? The minister also reports to the house for the C.B.C. and after hearing him, I feel that he should be a member of the C.B.C. performers' guild, for he introduced this legislation, which he knows to be of vital importance, with a nonchalance implying that the bill contained nothing important.
The fact remains, though, that this bill is a superlatively protectionist step, and is well in line with Conservative tradition.
It has been said in certain quarters that the Minister of National Revenue was no more enthused over the prospect of introducing this legislation than was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), but that the Prime Minister was anxious that it be brought forward at this time in order to prove that, though he had been a Liberal until 1928, he has really become a one hundred per cent Tory. In fact, if we study the history of the Conservative party, we will see that it has at all times identified itself with protectionism. When the party was being led by Sir John A. Macdonald, it was a protectionist party but its protective legislation was introduced in the house itself, and it was the house and not the cabinet that arbitrarily decided upon a given tariff that set the valuation of goods for duty.

In those days Sir John A. Macdonald could well have definite reasons to follow a protectionist policy, because the population of this country was predominantly rural, to the extent of 70 per cent, and agriculture in those days was a family operation, and just enough was produced for personal requirements.
It will readily be understood that, in those days, customs duties were more a source of revenue for the country than a means of protecting industry, which, at the time was, to all practical purposes, inexistent, or very limited. The same thing held true about the United States. Indeed, at that time the United States, like Canada, had a protectionist policy because of the influence of its 70 per cent rural population. Today, the converse is true. The population of industrial cities represents about 70 per cent of the entire population, and even the farming industry-we describe it as such because it has achieved the status of industry-is comprised of all kinds of co-operatives which enable it to produce enough not only to provide for family needs but also to supply large national and international markets.
If Sir John A. Macdonald were back with us, I am convinced that, as a man of acknowledged superior intelligence, he would look upon tariff protection with a different eye than does the present Prime Minister.
Today, the government is taking devious means to reach an objective that they do not wish to admit. Tariffs are not being increased and we might be told in a moment, when the minister replies, that the government does not intend to raise tariffs and that this is meant simply to protect industries going through temporary difficulties. To my way of thinking, to adopt a particular tariff, or to provide under the bill for some way of arbitrarily setting the valuation for duty purposes of goods so that their price at entry will be higher than the original cost is in fact a tariff increase, even if the rate of duty is not raised.
If today the Conservative party chooses to use this roundabout way to introduce a protectionist policy, for which it is well known, it is because it fears representations from the west and from the maritimes which require foreign markets for their expansion, cannot be satisfied with domestic markets, and will have to seek foreign markets.
Under this bill, the minister is given unlimited powers. I will not deal with the sections of the bill, which is allowed only in

committee, but I find that the different sections are so drawn as to give to the hon. minister and to the government the power to increase the valuation of goods especially on the basis of their cost of production plus a profit.
The cost of production is something that is extremely hard to determine intelligently. Let us take the case of two manufacturers. One of them uses old methods and outdated machinery; he leaves his business to its fate, good or bad. As a consequence his cost of production is much higher than in the case of an industrialist who takes advantage of new methods and new machinery and keeps his business under close supervision. Thus, if the government were to abuse its arbitrary powers and wanted to protect a mismanaged industry, it would at the same time increase the revenue of well organized industries, that is of big industries because in most cases the lesser industries are the ones that are not so well organized.
In any event I feel I can say that this bill is the fulfilment of an election promise, even if the government does not dare admit it. That explains why this devious method is being used to invest the Minister of National Revenue with such extraordinary powers.
I have here a translation of an article published in Saturday Night for May 10 and signed by John A. Stevenson. I quote:
One hundred and seventeen out of the 208 Progressive Conservative members in the new parliament come from Ontario and Quebec. Most of these 117 have been elected under specific pledges to work for the better tariff protection of industries in their constituencies which are suffering from foreign competition, and the prevailing volume of unemployment will supply them with ammunition for fortifying their pressure upon the government for remedial action.
Accordingly there are signs that ministers are in a serious quandary about their policy in regard to trade and tariff. They know that any policy which gave the protectionist forces in the United States congress an excuse for passing damaging retaliatory legislation would be a very dangerous adventure and so they have been singing very low about the project for a diversion of our import trade. The Prime Minister has lately broken a long silence about it by an explanation that he had merely said that a diversion of 15 per cent from the United States to Britain would cure the present lack of equilibrium in Canada's balance of trade with the United States and whoever had represented him as having given an explicit pledge to accomplish this had been guilty of what Sir Winston Churchill once called "a terminological inexactitude."
And further:
Every Tory member for a seat which has a textile plant within its bounds will be aggrieved if some succor in the form of higher duties is not forthcoming when Mr. Fleming submits his first budget.
Customs Act
This article therefore clearly states that the devious way in which things are being done at this time is designed to avoid irritating the west, irritating the east, irritating those extremists which come from the central provinces, Quebec and Ontario. In any event, every time a Conservative government has been in power the same thing has never failed to happen. The same devious method was always resorted to in order to achieve that end.
And still farther on:
At the moment the Canadian Tariff Board is working overtime to deal with an abnormal flood of applications for higher protection for domestic industries.
In 1921, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) pointed out a few minutes ago, the same legislation was passed, under which the minister was given power to establish the value of production costs, and to add a reasonable profit. That is mainly what makes this legislation bad. We do not object to the minister having certain powers, but if he is enabled to exercise those powers for increasing tariffs, without this house or the Canadian people being informed, I say that this is wrong, and that we should therefore not support the legislation.
The Liberal party had to revoke the act in 1922. However, exactly the same legislation was enacted in 1930 by the Bennett administration, when the tariff was based on the valuation of production costs plus a set profit. Moreover, the minister had some discretionary powers which went beyond all limits; it was a protectionist power. Anyhow, as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) said on another occasion, "What are production costs?" They may be anything and everything. This is perfectly true, and how will the minister be able to establish the value of a product in an efficient way at the best possible price?
Is it up to the government to protect an industry which does not look after its own business? Is it up to the government to protect an industry which is not well organized? No, but it is up to the government to safeguard an organized industry, not only so as to enable the owner to make a profit but so that those who are buying the goods may also benefit. Even the best government cannot be, any more than is the minister, in a position to determine a reasonable production cost with a reasonable profit. That is why we are opposed to the passage of this bill, as were the Liberals in 1921 and in 1930,

Customs Act
since we recall that in 1922 and in 1935, they had to repeal those bills, otherwise the United States would have kept on establishing tariffs themselves, as a reprisal measure against Canadian trade. Besides, that was one of the reasons for clause 38 of the former Bennett bill, which the Liberals wanted to repeal in 1948, in connection with British preferential treatment. Today, this provision is being kept in the bill, precisely through arbitrary powers granted to the minister, with regard to the determination of production cost, as well as through arbitrary powers placed in the hands of the minister, with regard to the determination of that cost and the establishment of related tariffs. This bill, therefore, ignores British preferential treatment.
Besides, let us not forget that Canada is an exporting country, which produces much more than it is able to consume. Canada needs markets, and if every change in government must give rise to difficulties as a result of the establishment by the party in power, through devious means such as this, of a protection tariff, I think unemployment, resentment and hardship will follow. A measure like this was adopted in 1921, and was followed by a slight business slump. Thank God, Canada put the Liberal party back into office, and the party created new markets after opening up the older ones. Unfortunately, in 1930, Mr. Bennett came back into power with his slogan that he was going to "blast his way into the world markets" through those devious means, and we saw what the consequences were for Canada.
Furthermore, advantage is always taken of any slackening in the tempo of business to have these same arbitrary measures and methods adopted. I put it to you squarely that I am concerned for Canada; I fear our industry will not be able to go on selling its products abroad, and that this will give rise to a production surplus, and a production surplus will give rise to unemployment. And when you get unemployment, the way to meet it is not to adopt that sort of measure, any more than to hand out unemployment insurance on a silver platter, but to clear the way for the marketing of our goods so that we have no surplus.
There has been talk lately of the important problem of textile products. The textile industry is exposed to difficulties, and is having trouble in riding the storm. Is it because of overproduction? Or dumping? I say no.
