speechtext:
The textile industry is going through a bad period. It is not by means of arbitrary measures like this one that we shall end the problem. It is all very well to be able to help the industry with this measure, but what is the use of doing so if it means throttling the country's economy in the process? To begin with, the textile industry is in difficulties in Canada, just like it is in the United States, England, Italy and indeed the whole world. Markets have changed, conditions are different, and one of the main difficulties confronting the textile industry arises from its having come into being in Canada at a time when communications facilities were poor and we hardly produced enough for ourselves. Today, however, there are fine communications facilities throughout the world, and the textile industry is in difficulties because, to begin with, we in Canada lack the raw materials, we have to import them from abroad, we must shoulder the transportation costs, and then re-export the finished product. Accordingly, production costs and sales prices are higher, and we have a hard time competing with prices prevailing on the American market. Indeed, the American market has had its own difficulties. Manufacturers in the state of Maine moved their industry to the south of the United States so as to be closer to the source of their raw materials because of dual transportation costs and some American industries even moved to South America.
We cannot solve this problem by adopting this arbitrary provision proposed by the government. Setting the cost of production against the market value is really bad and arbitrary powers conferred upon the minister are hardly any better. Encroachment upon the rights of parliament is the reason why we cannot accept this measure and why this amendment was moved.
When he was in the opposition the Prime Minister used to stand in the defence of rights of parliament whereas, today, he would

have us confer arbitrary powers upon the minister and the government. After censuring government by orders in council, he is the first one to resort to this method.
He, the first to condemn such a practice, gives his ministers powers which never before in Canada were exercised even by Conservative ministers. This we must oppose because it constitutes a threat to our trade with the world. Moreover, it is incompatible with the Geneva agreements and may lead to all sorts of difficulties in our trade with several countries. It is not in accordance with the spirit of GATT. While imposing on other countries, by indirect means, higher tariffs on the importation of goods into Canada, even though it may be contrary to the spirit of GATT, we do not like to see other countries react in the same way and resort to the same means for their own protection.
Well, here is one section which goes far enough since it states:
Where the minister is satisfied that material injury has been or may be-
Those words are beyond me.
-caused to any industry.
This means that when the minister thinks some prejudice may be caused, he has by that very fact the right to order the enactment of a tariff equal to production costs which will make the importation of some foreign commodity to this country practically impossible.
Section 38 says:
The value for duty shall be deemed to have been duly fixed by the minister pursuant to subsection (1) if the same is fixed on a basis or by a method prescribed by the minister.
That is to say not in the manner it should normally be dealt with on the world market, but by a method prescribed by the minister. It is inconceivable that the government should think of such an action, more particularly after everything that had been said by our hon. friends opposite especially during the last few sessions. Heaven knows how shocked they were when they were sitting on the other side of this house and the Liberal government was ruling by order in council. And now they themselves want to impose their point of view in this matter.
If you look the budget speech over again, you will see that the Minister of Finance announced that he wanted to determine the production cost plus a reasonable amount for gross profit. His mind was therefore made up even before the election! As it was said in an article published in Saturday Night, that
Customs Act
decision was taken to please some members from Ontario and Quebec. The production cost was going to be established, plus a reasonable profit, but nobody wanted to ask for a raise of tariffs in this house because nobody wanted to displease people both east and west. The minister may well answer that the fair market value can be fictitious. That may be so. But nobody will ever find a way to know what the market value will be in other countries. We know it in the case of British articles imported in this country. We knew their market value; we know their value on the English market; if we didn't know, we could easily find out by asking the Board of Trade in London. But who is going to tell us how to determine the cost of production plus profit? And if you leave it in the hands of the minister, and he does whatever he wants to do, unbeknownst to parliament, what will happen? The Canadian people might very well pay more without knowing why, and without the house being told why!
Here is the definition of dumping in section 35:
Sale in Canada of goods at a lower price than the fair market value on the main market of the exporting country.
I know it is not too difficult to determine fair market value, but when it is claimed that the tariff is the cause of disquiet in the textile industry, I cannot help quoting the following article by Grant Dexter, in the Winnipeg Free Press:
(Text):
The tariff board report showed that the Canadian woollen mills were in difficulty but that the cause did not lie with imports. The chief causes were: More intense competition from synthetic fabrics and the heavy loss on inventory due to the fall in prices in 1953-54.
(Translation):
I could go on and give clear proof that, even according to the tariff board, textiles are not in that position.
We are asked at this time to give arbitrary power to support the textile industry, or so it is claimed. But who is to say where those in authority will stop? Who will tell us if, under pressure, the minister will not be induced to act in a way in which he would not normally act? He is as human as anybody else, and the cabinet ministers form a group who, like the rest of us, are subject to bargaining and to political difficulties. In order to make friends, they might well act in a way in which they would not act if they had to render a frank and honest accounting to parliament in this respect.

Customs Act
Well, we of the opposition have fought this legislation today because the point at issue is a transfer to the government of the powers of parliament. How will the cost of production be determined? Nobody knows. The Department of National Revenue as well as the Minister of National Revenue are quick in admitting that the cost of production may be anything at all. Since there is agreement on that score and since the minister is being vested here with arbitrary powers, it does seem to me that the government should accept the amendment put forward at this time and which is designed, to a certain extent at least, to change part of what we are asked to approve. In fact, the very principle of the bill endangers all those agreements which, up to now, have benefited this country.
Canada is an exporting country. As such it cannot afford to let the minister endanger our foreign trade by indulging in arbitrary decisions.
Personally I am somewhat inclined to free trade. I wonder why, with the arbitrary power which is being given the minister, how he will be able to meet with British parliamentarians with representatives of the government of the United Kingdom, when they will arrive in Montreal later this month to discuss agreements with the Canadian government, especially if account is taken of the fact that they have already suggested free trade.
Those people are not fools and, upon reading the bill, they will soon discover its hidden faults.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this matter from another standpoint altogether. The hon. minister is a lawyer and he may, like his other legal confreres in the house, appreciate what puzzles me. It is one thing to write a law; it is another thing to interpret it and to apply it. It is quite simple for the minister to write regulations but I wonder whether he has ever given thought to his colleagues on the bench who may be called upon to interpret those regulations. It is from that standpoint that I should like to speak.
I am not critical of the draftsmanship of the bill but I confess I find it extremely difficult to understand the various clauses of the legislation. I address myself to all members of the house irrespective of the side they are sitting on, and ask them whether they can say in all honesty and frankness that they have read all the various clauses of this bill and understood them. I find it very difficult to vote for a measure which I must honestly admit I do not understand. There are clauses set up at great length consisting of one sentence sometimes extending over two pages, and by the time one reaches the end one cannot trace any connection with the beginning. I do not want to think of myself as

a representative of the society for the prevention of cruelty to lawyers and to judges nor do I want to suggest that the members of the bar who may have to deal with these clauses will need to take post graduate law courses in Philadelphia, but that is the way I look at this legislation. Let me quote, as one illustration, clause 40 which is a relatively brief clause:
Where sufficient information has not been furnished or is not available-
I underline those words "and is not available".
-to enable the determination of cost of production, gross profit or fair market value under section 36, 37 or 39, the cost of production, gross profit or fair market value, as the case may be, shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if such information is not available will the minister assume the role of having divine power and being a seer? Where will the minister get the information to determine this cost if the information is not available? That question, Mr. Speaker, a judge on a bench may at some time have to determine. The information is not available, and that is why I say in all frankness that sometimes I cannot understand the legislation. The measure points out in one clause after another-it is the protective phrase which runs all through this legislation-that where it is not possible to determine value it shall be done in such a manner as the minister prescribes.
It would have been a simple matter for the minister to have written this law by saying the value shall be determined as the minister prescribes, and nothing else. What is the purpose of writing a full page of a clause which then concludes by saying: "If this is not possible, the minister shall determine the method by which value should be established". It would have been simpler to have written one sentence: "Value for duty purposes shall be that which the minister shall prescribe or determine."
Similarly, on the question of appeal, I see that section 45 is repealed and replaced, and reference is made to appeals on a question of law. I address myself directly to the minister. A man is entitled to appeal on a question of law. Is it a question of law to determine cost of production? That is purely a question of fact. It is almost an elementary question of fact. Cost of production is not a question of law. If it is so difficult to determine cost of production why should one not have the right to appeal on a question of production cost?
Fair market value is not a question of law. The minister will surely admit that fair market value is a question of fact after
Customs Act
determining a great many elements which go into the determination of fair market value. Why should not one be permitted to appeal a matter of fact such as fair market value?
Let us consider gross profit. Is that a question of law? It is not a simple matter from all these clauses to determine how gross profit will be established. If it is so difficult to establish gross profit the procedure of establishing it can be only by examining the facts. Why should not one be permitted to appeal the question of gross profit? The same thing applies to value for duty. It seems to be referred to very frequently and is almost the basis of the entire measure.
In my dealings with the department I have found the departmental officials most cooperative, congenial and anxious to serve. If a member of parliament can express a preference as to what department out of all the departments of government he prefers to deal with, my choice would certainly be the Department of National Revenue and the customs branch. I find them most cooperative. I also find, however, that they are placed on the spot in having to interpret. I do not like to press them for various interpretations. I believe the minister should not have created such a complicated vehicle to attain the objective he seeks. The protectionist objective could have been achieved in four or five sentences rather than in page after page of complex clauses that are practically all one sentence. He makes it extremely difficult for the officials of the department. I know they will have further difficulty in interpreting. They are constantly trying to divine what is in the mind of the minister.
I wish I could understand this measure. If I could I would perhaps deal with it in another fashion. Although I agree with everything my leader has said about the merits of this type of legislation and the principle which underlies it, in view of the fact that the legislation is not clear and is most confusing I cannot vote for it. Perhaps it was intended to be confusing and if it represents an attempt to cover up something the minister wishes to say but cannot say directly, I must say that not understanding the law I cannot in all good conscience vote for it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address myself fairly directly to the amendment that has been proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I hope to take another opportunity, perhaps in committee, to discuss some other aspects of tariffs and protection. I quite well realize that pressure is increasing in the country when there is something in the nature of a recession to keep out foreign goods. This amendment is not concerned with

Customs Act
the problem of dumping. Dumping is a cry that is always raised by protectionists whenever they cannot meet certain situations on merit.
What we are discussing with respect to this amendment is a question of parliamentary authority over the fundamental principle of taxation something I suggest we should be zealously guarding at all times. The power to tax traditionally belongs to parliament and not to a minister or the executive and that is the main point, as I see it, in the amendment that has been advanced and which is before us at the moment.
The new government is proposing to go back to the experience with which most of us are familiar and one that was associated with the previous Conservative administration under Mr. Bennett. I would suggest to hon. members of the government, particularly those from constituencies in western Canada and the maritimes, that if the electors in those areas had any idea that the result of the election would be a return to arbitrary valuations such as they rejected so emphatically in 1935 the outcome of the election would not have been as it was on March 31. I suggest that those hon. members whose geography I know best who come from the prairie provinces should give very careful consideration to this.
I should like to draw to the attention of certain hon. members and particularly those from sections of the country where primary industry depends on trade the desirability of considering some of the practical results of this policy when it was promoted in the thirties under the last Conservative administration. I have in my hand a rather classic and up to date textbook with respect to customs administration in Canada, written by Gordon Blake, and appearing as one of the Canadian studies in economics, No. 9 of the series. At pages 102 and 103 of this volume which is an analysis of our tariff system under the heading "Reaction Against Administrative Protection", when reviewing the situation in the thirties, the author states:
Official valuations were used also to impose very heavy duties on textiles. Values were listed on the basis of cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit, which in turn was based on the New York spot raw cotton price of seven cents per pound.
I wish to give illustrations of what happened before and after the issuing of a departmental letter of April 7, 1932. That is all it was but it represented the power to tax. Speaking of this the author states:
A departmental letter of April 7, 1932, to collectors and appraisers gave instruction as to values for duty to be applied to various qualities of cotton fabrics, when imported from the United States.

Here is the result. The figures are taken from invoices that appeared in evidence before the United States tariff commission when they were, under their more liberal trade policy, prepared to exclude Canada from any of the benefits of that new policy. Prior to the letter we had an invoice value in Canadian currency on a textile imported on April 6, 1932, of $55.32. I shall not go into the detail of how the duty was calculated but the total duties, regular, special and excise tax, amounted to $28.69, still a very substantial portion of the invoice value of the goods. Then, a month later, following this mere writing of a letter with no authority from parliament other than parliament surrendering its authority by giving it to a minister, on May 8, 1932, on goods with an invoice value in Canadian currency of $51.66 the total duties, regular, special, and excise tax amounted to $49.08, approaching the full value of the goods.
This is in practical form what results when parliament surrenders its rights to decide upon the over-all levels of taxation and certainly a tariff levy is a tax. It is a tax immediately on the importer but the importer, as we all know, immediately passes that tax on to the ultimate consumer. I suggest it is important that this government and paricularly its backbenchers should consider that they now have the largest majority that has ever been returned to parliament in the history of this country and there is nothing to stop them expressing out in the open and in a proper legislative form their views as to what tariff rates should be. I suggest it is completely improper for them to remain silent in this respect and I again point out that the electors in many parts of Canada would not have elected them if they felt the government they support was going to use this back door method.
I suggest that it is perfectly proper to indicate to the administration what these rates on these commodities should be. It should be made known; it should be something of public knowledge; it should be the law of the land and not something that is a back door, hole in the corner, secretive, arbitrary type of taxing solely at the discretion of the Minister of National Revenue.
There are strong feelings with respect to this type of taxation and impost of cost, which I say are very quickly passed on in the form of cost on working men's overalls, or the cost of children's clothing, or those various things. This is something of utmost importance. I do not think I have read a better expression concerning this right to tax than an article which appeared in the Victoria Times of July 30, which had this to say:
Foreign goods must not be sold here-

Apparently it had reference to announcements which were forecast in the budget. I continue:
-unless their selling price is as high as the cost of production, plus a reasonable profit.
How can the cost of production be determined? Will every foreign manufacturer tell the Canadian government how much he is spending on production or what profit margin he is earning? Of course not. Besides, the production costs and profits of every manufacturer are different.
Since the facts are unobtainable, the government will dream them up for itself. It will guess what it costs to produce a certain article, it will add an imagined reasonable profit and then levy import duties on the resulting figure.
Now, as I say, addressing myself simply to the amendment, I want to ask hon. members, particularly those from the prairie provinces and the maritimes and from northern Ontario, where we produce almost entirely for export markets, and in the past on a large and expanding two-way trade, whether or not they really want to vote for something that is hole in the corner, back room administration, resulting in taxation by simply writing a letter, as the most practical thing that might be the law of the land rather than a tariff rate expressed by parliamentary vote.

speechtext:
I do not intend to make a speech, either. In fact, what I intend to do mainly is to repeat a part of an excellent speech made in this house 28 years ago by another Liberal, sitting at that time in opposition, which I happened on and which I would add is far better than I could have done myself. But I wanted to say, first, Mr. Speaker, that after I read the bill, which is now before the house, I remembered the great interest that the Prime Minister always took when he was on this side of the house in King Charles' head which is relevant to the question which is before us now. The minister will remember, of course, that King James I, when he sought to liberate himself from the financial control of parliament, hit upon the bright idea that since duties were a tax on foreigners and not on the subjects they were not under the control of parliament. The Minister of National Revenue, of course, remembers the history of a merchant named Bate who was seeking to import currants. This became a very celebrated case in parliament and it led ultimately, in King Charles' time of course, to different and other methods of trying to get around parliamentary control of taxation.
Customs Act
It led to the famous provision in the petition of right which I do not hesitate to mention here, sir, because it is one of the great charters of our liberties which I understand we are going to seek to confirm or start confirming later in the present week. It is something odd that as a prelude to that confirmation we should have this deliberate front door attempt to take the control over taxation away from parliament.
I really was tempted to get up to speak on this mainly by the fact that, in the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia, the ghost of the progressive party walked through this house this afternoon with Mr. Meighen's temporary cloak over him. It was very interesting to hear what I suppose, if one went through all his speeches, must have been the only Liberal speech that Mr. Meighen ever made. I daresay it was made purely as revenge because his arbitrary legislation of the year before was being taken off the statute books. At the time that other legislation was put on, Mr. Ian Mackenzie said, as reported at page 257 of Hansard of September 16, 1930, in seconding Mr. Stewart's motion, to which reference was made earlier this afternoon, and what is completely relevant to the matter before us:
This legislation definitely deprives parliament of all control over our system of taxation in Canada. The fabric of our taxation system in this dominion, as in other countries, is concerned with our revenues and expenditures. What is the situation? By section 4 we are delegating to the cabinet council of Canada the complete right and authority to fix valuation, without limitation, on any article whatsoever imported into the dominion.
I am going to leave out a bit because it really has not any relevancy and go on:
The only argument adduced by the minister- The minister on that occasion had adduced a little more in the way of argument than the minister has adduced today. I continue: The only argument adduced by the minister in defence of this legislation is the tu quoque argument;-
Apparently, Tory governments never change. They either say, "You did it or you did not do it". That is their argument. I continue: The only argument adduced by the minister in defence of this legislation is the tu quoque argument; he says, "You hon. gentlemen, when you sat to the right of the Speaker introduced a special section 43, or section 37a,-
That is the section on natural products to which the hon. member for Assiniboia referred this afternoon. Mr. Mackenzie went on: -whatever it may have been, and you gave the same authority with regard to natural products." Now, although I do believe that the fruit industry of British Columbia is in need of protection, I believe at the same time that there may be far better remedies to meet the difficulties of the fruit growers of British Columbia than giving them the protection which is given by this government.

Customs Act
That is very similar to what was said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) with reference to textiles. Then, Mr. Mackenzie went on:
I am opposed to the principle of the old section 43, or 47a. I do not believe that parliament should give up its supreme authority and delegate it to any cabinet council, be it Liberal or Conservative, farmer or labour.
As I imagined the minister intended to refer to this matter when he replied, I thought it desirable to put on the record now that Mr. Ian Mackenzie in 1930, speaking for the Liberal party, repented at that time and we think he was right to take the position he took at that time. He took the position that the legislation of 1922 was objectionable, not as objectionable as this bill, but it was objectionable, and we agree.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This bill for the relief of Kenneth Herbert Gregory is another bill which has brought before the house many of the faults and failings of the committee handling these bills. In this particular case a number of things occurred which should not have occurred in normal procedure. The Senate committee when hearing this particular case-and it is a contested case-heard evidence on clauses 12 and 14. It will be noticed that there are 16 clauses and that allegation No. 12 reads as follows:
That on October 29, 1957, respondent committed adultery with the said Ernest Meyers at the Tudor hotel, 599 Shelberne street, in the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario.
And No. 14 reads:
That on Monday, April 28, 1958, respondent committed adultery with the said Ernest Meyers at the Queen's hotel in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec.
Senate report No. 239 discusses the allegations contained in clauses 12 and 14. The clause following the allegations reads:
Wherefore your petitioner humbly prays that your honourable house

Well anyway it is not in that section.
Oh, oh.
Louder.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On page 8 the report says:
It was resolved to report to the main committee that:-"Your subcommittee find as a fact that, according to the evidence adduced, the allegations contained in paragraphs 1 to 16 both inclusive and particularly that the respondent committed adultery as alleged in paragraphs 11, 12, 13 and 14 of the said amended petition, have been proved."
It would appear to be rather difficult to find out from the report of the subcommittee of the Senate how the allegations in clauses 11 and 13 could have been proved, because
Private Bills
there was no evidence on those two particular allegations. They say that the allegations have been proved and that it was only fair and just that when an objection was made to the decision of the committee of the House of Commons they should be able to re-open this case on these two allegations which they had not previously discussed and that when they presented these allegations then they could come before the House of Commons committee. They brought evidence through new witnesses and presumably the evidence of those witnesses must have been the evidence on which the case was decided.
This, in my opinion, points up one problem facing the committee which should certainly be resolved before the committee sits again, for here we have the Senate ruling on divorce procedure and handling a case while hearing two allegations out of four and yet ruling on four of them that they had been proved, therefore making it necessary when an appeal was made on the two allegations which had not been heard before the House of Commons committee, that they should be able to reopen the case. I feel this is unfair to the House of Commons and it is unfair to the people involved. It is unfair to Mr. Gregory and to Mrs. Gregory, both of whom are involved in this case. They are being tried on two allegations and the decisions are made on those allegations, which are re-investigated before the house and a decision is made and then the case is again re-opened. Then we hear two different allegations which were not discussed at any length previously. We hear from witnesses on the second two allegations and in this case a different decision is arrived at.
In arriving at this decision another question was brought to light and that is that neither of the two lawyers, who are considered competent lawyers, both the lawyer for the petitioner and the lawyer for the respondent, after hearing the evidence on the second two allegations, presented very much of a case. It could be inferred, I think, because of the fact that cross-examination was not conducted as it had been in the previous allegations, that a settlement had probably been arrived at, and this was the reason for the basis of the divorce. If this is so I think the section here which says the petitioner in no way connived at or condoned the adultery committed by the respondent and that no collusion exists between the petitioner and the respondent to obtain a dissolution of the marriage does not apply if there was an arrangement between the petitioner and the respondent I suggest there was collusion in that case and that this section of the Senate evidence was disproven.

Private Bills-Divorce
It has been said in one of our recent cases, I assume it was this one, that these two people have no intention of living together again and therefore we should do the charitable thing and dissolve the marriage as they were asking. I do not think we are constituted as a committee to grant this divorce simply because the two people are not going to live together and I do not think we should be in a position where we are going to do it because the settlement is satisfactory or not.
This case points out another problem: are the petitioner and the respondent fit people to obtain a private bill in this House of Commons. The evidence of the petitioner in this case indicated certain facts to the committee. I believe everybody who heard the petitioner was not too impressed with his sincerity or his mental attitude and there may be some justification for the fact that this lady is now an alcoholic and has been treated on a number of occasions for this affliction. It could be suggested that part of the affliction from which this lady is now suffering was a result of the years during which she lived with this particular man.
In the second case where we heard the last two allegations on sections 11 and 13, there was a lady who testified as to the adultery having taken place. Her evidence before cross-examination was very good evidence, I should say. She testified very straightforwardly, remembering the complete case, the hours, the dates and the times. She was very concise and straightforward in her particulars of the case. It was only after the lawyer concerned failed to crossexamine her to any extent, and her own lawyer did not lead her in any direction, that the members of the committee did ask a number of questions and establish the fact that though she remembered these particulars very well she did not remember some of the other things. It was brought out by the committee that the petitioner in this case had contacted this lady within a few days of her appearing before us and discussed the case with her, and the implication was that arrangements had been made for her to testify in this case. If this is so I think it points out another implication that collusion did take place in this particular case.
Shame.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was not involved in the collusion. I think, the house should feel ashamed if they are going to pass this type of case and I think it points out the need for a closer examination of these cases. In my opinion if the lawyers in these cases are not going to carry them to a conclusion

and I think the committee will agree there was very little questioning on the latter allegations, there is always in people's minds the opportunity for the inference that there may have been some arrangement arrived at.
I think that this man does not deserve this divorce but I do think that probably the adultery charge has been proven. Certainly it was not disproved by the committee. I think the committee should have the right to make the decision in the first place and that when these allegations are cited the case must rest on the allegations they attempt to prove in the first place. If there are any allegations left over those allegations cannot be reheard because it would appear that if you are going to have a contested divorce you are going to be hearing these cases eight or ten times if they want to put in seven or eight allegations and have them heard each time. I am sure the chairman would agree that we do not want to get into a position that we got into this time where we are going to hear allegations that were not heard before.
Again it points out that when we are hearing new witnesses evidence should be taken down so that a final dispensation on the evidence can be made if the need should appear from something that happened later. The evidence should be taken down in a written form as it is now in the Senate. Also, we should have some direction on this committee from the House of Commons in setting up and constituting it. If we are going to have these divorce cases, as we have, we are going to have to have some pattern set up which will enable us to handle them in a proper manner and this particularly points this up. If we think that the man is not a fit subject to obtain a divorce I think the committee should obtain direction along that line. That should be part of the direction given to the committee when it is constituted the next time.
I am of the opinion that this particular case is a case where the allegations have not been completely proved. I am not satisfied in my mind that these people should have a divorce. I would say that we did not in my opinion prove or disprove the evidence that was given in the last two allegations in obtaining the divorce, so for that reason we are not objecting to the passing of this particular bill.

The hon. member who has just spoken has made several points before the House of Commons which, if he had held a strong enough opinion on them, could have been made equally well before the committee.

There is the question of the character of the petitioner in this case, and whether the character of the petitioner was such as to entitle him to come before parliament and ask for relief. That was the ground on which the respondent's lawyers originally made an objection, but later it was withdrawn. In my handling of this case before the committee, before the evidence was completed and before the petitioner left the room I told the committee that if anyone had any questions regarding the man's merit to receive a divorce I would see that those questions were answered by the man when he was before us. When the committee came to consider its decision-a decision which was unanimous and included the vote of the hon. member who just sat down-that point was raised and no vote was taken upon it. We then dealt with the prime issue of the case, whether the allegation of adultery had been proven and we disposed of that, again unanimously.
On the matter of the procedure followed, it is perfectly true as the hon. member pointed out that the petitioner had two bites at this case. First, the hotel evidence. The two allegations were disposed of. Second, on the instruction of the House of Commons, where the hon. member might have made his objection, it came back before us and we heard evidence concerning two other allegations. I have learned something from that experience. Next year when we have counsel before us in these contested cases if they are going to rely on only two allegations out of a number of allegations they will be asked to either give positive evidence on the other allegations or close off their cases at that point so the experience we had this year will not be encountered in similar circumstances next year.
Some emphasis was laid by the hon. member on the question of collusion. It is an unhappy fact in divorce law that two parties cannot get together and enter into a written agreement on separation. Legal action has to be taken in that regard subsequent to the divorce being granted. In this particular case the lawyer acting for the petitioner and the lawyer acting for the respondent came before me. We discussed the matter at some length. It was clearly stated by these men who are reputable Queen's Counsel that no such agreement could possibly exist. It was unfortunate. They would have liked to have seen one exist in this case because the woman involved was an alcoholic and will obviously need some care before this chronic condition of hers is overcome. But the state of the law being as it is these lawyers could not make an agreement which would have been beneficial to the parties concerned, would have made the 57071-3-284
Private Bills-Divorce
task of our committee a much happier one and would have been of benefit to society as well.
There is no possible evidence of collusion and to raise that question in the House of Commons is to question the reputations of two reputable lawyers by suggesting that they acted in a way in which they could not have acted and continue to maintain their standing in the bar associations of their respective provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
If, as the hon. member who just sat down states, there has been no settlement in this case then I would oppose the passing of this bill. I would assume there has been some arrangement made. I failed to ask that question in the committee and therefore I am partly to blame for not being able to say there had been some type of settlement in this case. If there was no agreement between the two parties-and we can only guess about that-then I am very much opposed to the divorce being granted on the simple ground that this woman will be left completely dependent on the mercies of the province in which she lives or whoever may be looking after her welfare. I am of the opinion she still has a serious medical problem that remains to be solved. I would submit that this problem is not entirely her own responsibility. From my encounter with the petitioner I believe some of the blame must be shared by him.
There is another matter about cases of this kind which I shall not discuss at length. I have no objection to what the lawyers do in these cases. After all, they are in this type of business and it is a smart business. The lawyer reopened the case on certain grounds. In my opinion he would have been well advised not to have pursued the matter. He knew it could not be pursued to any extent. I think the other lawyer felt the same way about the matter and did not pursue it but I believe some hon. members of this house who are members of the medical profession would have liked to have gone into the matter.
This case illustrates the problems we have to face. If we are going to hear divorce cases we should have a certain procedure to follow. The Senate has a procedure which it follows and a set pattern under which it operates but the House of Commons does not operate under that type of pattern. In my opinion we should be advised of settlements in these cases. If by means of a private bill we are going to dissolve a marriage after a number of years we should have the opportunity of making an assessment of the situation and assuring that an arrangement is made for the continued support of the woman in the case.

Private Bills
If the hon. member who just took his seat is saying that no decision has been made I would be very much opposed to the divorce being granted. I am not asking him to say that. He does not have to defend the lawyers. It is my personal opinion-as his was a personal opinion-that a settlement has been arrived at in the case. Although it would be nice to keep these people together so they could not ruin the lives of other people I think we should grant the divorce.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, 1 have to answer that point. When we discussed this matter with the lawyers they said no written settlement had been reached between them. The husband has some amount of money and if after the divorce because of his wife's alcoholic condition he wished to make some financial provision for her that course would always be open to him but there could be no agreement reached between them beforehand or that would have constituted collusion.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know any of the facts in this case nor do I know the parties but I am rising as a result of a statement made by the hon. member for Timiskaming. If I correctly understood his remarks he made a statement that creates something of a paradox for the House of Commons. He appeared to insinuate that there may have been some sort of collusion or some sort of deal made between the lawyers that a divorce be granted. The hon. member constantly used the word settlement and said that a settlement was made as a result of which he would like to see the divorce granted.
I do not know if I correctly understood the ambiguous remarks of the hon. member but they appear to create a paradox for parliament. Under the law if there had been any collusion or if a deal had been made between the parties for a divorce to be granted the hon. member cannot properly say he will vote for the granting of that divorce. I do not know who were the solicitors in the case but I certainly do not think we should reasonably allow a reflection to be cast on them to the effect that a deal had been made and as a consequence parliament will grant the divorce.
The chairman of the committee on miscellaneous private bills assured this committee that no such indication was given and that indeed no collusion existed between the parties and that would be a better basis on which to pass this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am standing in for the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) who unfortunately was injured in a motor accident today and I would like to proceed. I therefore move the second reading of Bill No.S-15, respecting Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited.

Mr. Speaker, this company has had a most interesting life history since 1952. Those hon. members who were in the house at that time will recall that the charter legislation sought by this company in 1952, and later, was most vigorously opposed by prominent members of the present government, by some members of the Liberal party and by the members of the C.C.F. Those who were here at that time will recall that there were some very interesting and at times caustic debates surrounding this legislation. For the information of the newer members who might not know the background and the history of this company which has presented this bill to the house for its consideration at this time, may I say I have taken some pains to prepare some rather careful notes so that I will condense the telling of the history of this company in as short a space as possible. After doing that I intend to quote from the speeches of various members of the government to illustrate to the house how they fought at that time for the protection of the interests of the Canadian people.
From our point of view, Mr. Speaker, and I think from the point of view of those gentlemen who opposed this pipe line bill so vigorously in years past, the history of this company is not particularly good. This bill marks the third separate and distinct proposal that this company has made to parliament.
The first occasion was in 1952, when, under the name of the Boundary Pipe Line Corporation, this company came before parliament with a bill that would have authorized them to construct a pipe line within Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba or outside of Canada. Their declared aim at that time was to pipe natural gas from the area near

Medicine Hat to Winnipeg, with the possibility of exporting gas to a United States pipe line company from that point.
The next year they came before the house with a new bill masquerading under a new name, something like political parties do on occasions, the Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited, and a new proposal, namely to build an all-Canadian pipe line to transport natural gas from Alberta to central Canada. Actually, this new proposal seemed to be a mere gambit, in my opinion, in order to secure the approval of the House of Commons and the passage of the bill, for evidence before the House of Commons committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines shows that the company had not spent any money on economic surveys, and so forth, other than, if I remember correctly, the $25,000 that had been spent before the 1952 bill was presented to this house. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) was most critical of the bill at that time and on a later occasion, on March 3, the present Minister of Public Works had this to say:
I believe it was felt last year by many members of the house that these applicants were merely trying to get a charter for its nuisance value. If they could get a charter and then by hook or crook get permission to export gas from Alberta ahead of other pipe line companies, they would be in position to call the tune. There would be no doubt that they would have a most valuable asset. I believe the same position exists today with these applicants applying again for a charter.
This was on their second application. I continue:
Another ground on which we opposed the application last year was that the gas was to be taken to the United States.
It seems rather clear that this new attempt to secure powers to build a pipe line outside of Canada has a similar motive. When the bill was in the House of Commons committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in 1953 it was amended on the motion of the present Minister of Public Works and various words which the company now wants restored were struck out. The bill was amended at that time to prevent the company from doing the very thing that it proposes to do in the bill before the house at this ime. I remember very well how prominent members of the government, prominent members of the party and the former leader of the Progressive Conservative party fought this proposal most heartily. A sidelight is that as the company's parliamentary agent, Mr. D. K. MacTavish, said at the time these amendments were quite acceptable to the promoters. He said that the amendments proposed by the members on this side who were opposing the bill were quite acceptable then. What I want to know is, why are they no 57071-3-2841
Private Bills
longer acceptable? The reason lies in the failure of the promoters of this company to get the blessing of either the Alberta government or the federal government so far as the trans-Canada pipe line project is concerned.
The promoters were not able to capitalize on their nuisance value. As 1 understand it, they were not able to call the tune and so they have set their eyes on a different project. Now they come before parliament with their plan to build an oil pipe line from the Edmonton area to Chicago. Most of the pipe line companies have provisions restricting them from building pipe lines outside of Canada. The Interprovincial Pipelines is one exception. If Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited were able to get this bill through, then they would indeed be in a very powerful position-this is one point I want to bring to the attention of the house-if at any time in the future such a pipe line route becomes generally acceptable.
A bargaining position is certainly all that the promoters of this company are trying to attain. So far as the members of this group can understand, I do not think that anybody can pretend that access to the Chicago market could be obtained without deals with United States oil and pipe line interests that would almost certainly involve very substantial United States control of this company which proposes to transport Canadian natural resources. Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited may be a Canadian company now and it may propose to set up a wholly-owned subsidiary in the United States to operate that portion of the pipe line built in the United States, but we can be sure that if and when this project comes to reality the parent company would itself become United States-controlled. An example of the kind of thing that could happen is in Westcoast Transmission where, in order to obtain a large sales contract with Pacific Northwest Pipeline Corporation, the company was advised to sell Pacific Northwest Pipe Lines approximately 25 per cent of its stock, making the matter of Canadian control of this company a rather open and debatable question.
In order that new members of the house can understand the background of the bill and know the opinions expressed by prominent members of the government, the former leader of the Progressive Conservative party and prominent members of the Liberal party, I intend to quote from Hansard for the 195253 session. One gentleman whom I have pleasure in quoting on this occasion is the

Private Bills
present Minister of Public Works who had this to say as found on page 2582 of Hansard for March 3, 1953:
In effect, the only thing he has said is that if they get the charter they intend to build a gas pipe line from Alberta through different Saskatchewan centres to Manitoba; and then he said something to the effect that they intend to go on to eastern Canada. I must admit at the commencement of my remarks that if I really believed that was the intention of the applicants, I would have little objection to this bill. But because I do not think that is as yet their real intention, I propose to make a few remarks with regard to the bill.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra of that day went on to say:
A similar provision was written into last year's bill in committee; but unfortunately that provision does not mean very much, if anything, where a pipe line company proposes to run its line down to the United States boundary and then sell the gas to an associate company incorporated under the laws of the United States.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra of that day also said:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it has been said in this house, and I think rightly so, that although the government was elected on a Liberal ticket it has been administering the country with old and worn-out Tory policies with about the same alarming results which were obtained by previous Conservative administrations.

And more particularly it is evidenced in this bill to amend the Customs Act where under the guise of anti-dumping regulations the government is once again returning to the traditional Tory policy of protective trade barriers used by the Conservative administration decades ago with the deplorable results of which we are all aware.
We on this side of the house do not for a moment underestimate the dangers of dumping practices in this country, nor are we

against anti-dumping regulations which will effectively stop this very unfair and piratical form of trade.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
It is quite evident that the previous government was not against antidumping regulations because it included in its legislation under the Customs Tariff antidumping regulations and we are completely in favour of any legislation which might curb this very nefarious practice. We are, however, opposed to legislation which, under the guise of anti-dumping regulations, is in fact a not too subtle return by the government to Conservative protectionism against normal competition or competition which is known throughout the world as being on a fair basis. We are opposed, as we have been opposed for a good many years, to the Conservative theory which the government is apparently re-introducing by this bill of the evaluation of duty based on cost of production plus a reasonable amount of gross profit and where the minister has the widest discrimination of guessing what is the cost of production and what a reasonable amount for gross profit might conceivably be and then fixing a completely arbitrary value for duty on such goods as he may deem fit.
I submit that this legislation is no longer anti-dumping legislation but is laying the foundation for the old Conservative protectionist theory. It seems to me that we should remember the experience of the Conservatives with this type of legislation. History does not warrant for one single moment a return to that type of protection. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that everything points to the contrary, and that beween 1930 and 1935 I think everyone will agree that this same type of legislation was not at all successful. It did not for a moment protect industry, nor did it solve the unemployment problem of that time and it certainly did not help our export trade. As a matter of fact, it was detrimental to the export trade and moreover it increased the number of unemployed during that period and today, when all the nations of the world, even those who in the past have been most reluctant to do so, have embarked upon policies of freer and freer trade-

speechtext: Personally I do not believe that the basic cause of the textile industry's problem is low tariffs; I do not believe that the true solution to the textile problem lies in high tariff protection against normal competition. speechtext:
This does not mean that the government should not give assistance and encouragement to this very important and responsible industry in Canada, but it does mean that the government should give assistance which is more aggressive and more imaginative and that it should be aimed at making the industry itself more competitive and more economical, rather than offer, as this bill provides, a passive assistance by
Customs Act
protection which will in time stifle, smother and finally destroy the industry by making its existence impossible in this highly and increasingly competitive and hard-bargaining world.
I feel sure that Canadian manufacturers and industrialists realize, as we all do, that for some years now we have been witnessing a veritable revolution in world trade practices and policies. We see that we cannot successfully meet the serious challenge of new trading conditions by counting exclusively on the artificial and outdated forms of protection. Although I may scandalize certain people in this house and in the country I sincerely believe that the successful adaptation of the textile industry and other industries to present trading conditions can only be achieved after careful, complete, objective and honest scrutiny has been given to ascertain whether the industry either in whole or in part in its present form and with the present market is economically viable and sound.
If it is not, I submit that it is in the true interest of employees and manufacturers alike to face the situation as it really is and not as they would like it to be, and work together in order to change the method of production, the market or the product in order to make this industry economically sound and viable in present trading conditions. If the industry is economically sound and viable, then notwithstanding the serious difficulties and problems which now face it I submit that government, management and labour must consider together what steps should be taken to bring prices into line with those of other countries not only in Canada but on the world market. I feel that the basic problem facing the textile industry is not so much the problem of dumping but normal competition which is considered in the world as fair competition.
If the industry is to continue to exist I submit that normal competition must be met. There is really no easy way out of this problem. This bill, popular though it may be among some hon. members of the house and some people in certain industries in some areas, will not, in my opinion, solve the problem. It can only assure the complete disappearance of the industry by making it a misfit in present conditions and rendering it incapable of continued existence.
I believe that it is most unwise, most unsound and even dangerous for the government to assume, as it does in this bill, the role of protector of free enterprise at the expense of the general economy and by jeopardizing our vital export trade without giving in effect any real protection to the

Customs Act
industry. Of course, the government has a responsibility and a definite interest in helping those industries which are now in difficulty to readapt themselves to completely new conditions. That help should be sound, objective and effective and it should also be completely in accord with the true interest of the general economy of this country.
I do not pretend to be an expert on either the textile industry or the custom structure but I cannot help feel there must be some measure other than the unsuccessful and obsolete protectionist method embodied in this bill, which might offer a more effective solution to the problem, and which would be far more in keeping with our concept of free enterprise. It seems to me that if the government were to grant to the textile industry and to other affected industries an accelerated rate of depreciation allowance on machinery in order to permit the industry to reequip with the latest machinery and techniques so as to reduce the cost of production it would be a far more effective approach to this problem than the artificial protection contemplated in this bill.
I also believe that if the industries themselves lessened their diversification of production and concentrated on producing as cheaply as possible one or two qualities or patterns of goods in greater quantities they would be far more competitive than they are today. Then, through our Canadian trade missions throughout the world, the industry should cater to world trade. It should seek out potential world markets and organize themselves to compete in those markets with reduced diversification rather than cater to the home market exclusively with its limited purchasing power and its demand for highly diversified products. Most countries of the world have in recent years geared their industries to the home market, if you like, but with a keen and watchful eye on the world market and on world demand. In Canada, perhaps because our country is comparatively young, we have geared our industry to supplying the needs and tastes of the home market, despite its exigencies, neglecting the fact that the world market offers a great opportunity of stabilizing those industries which are now in difficulty if the necessary steps were taken to adapt the method or production and to set the cost of production in accordance with world demand rather than limiting operations to the very restricted and very exacting demands of the home market.
The former government foresaw this very marked trend toward freer and freer world trade, and because the former government did realize that the world market offered a very good solution to the problems which

are accompanying our economic expansion, Canada became not only a signatory to the general agreement on tariffs and trade but a very active and enthusiastic member of that extremely important international organization which I consider to be essential if we are to have free trade in the world. It may be useful to put on the record once again the introductory paragraph of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. After citing the different countries which are signatories to the agreement we read, and I quote:
These governments . . . recognizing that their relations in the field of trade and economic endeavour should be conducted with a view to raising standards of living, ensuring full employment and a large and steadily growing volume of real income and effective demand, developing the full use of the resources of the world and expanding the production and exchange of goods.
Being desirous of contributing to these objectives by entering into reciprocal and mutually advantageous arrangements directed to the substantial reduction of tariffs and other barriers to trade and to the elimination of discriminatory treatment in international commerce-
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of production formula which is the key note of this present bill for establishing value for duty is contrary to the objective and spirit of GATT, a portion of which I have just read. It is true that the present legislation does provide for the use of the cost of production method as a technique of last resort but under the present legislation we can have recourse to the cost of production method in evaluating duty only after we have gone through and exhausted the six or seven other methods that must be followed. Only when it is impossible to arrive at a value for duty, according to the present legislation, are we allowed to follow the cost of production method.
But under this bill the cost of production is given a competely new status. It is no longer a residual method of determining value for duty but is an alternative method under which the minister is no longer required to exhaust the other methods of determining value for duty but is given the widest discretion of guessing what the cost of production may be on certain items and imposing that as the value for duty.
I submit that this theory is a form of high tariff protection. It is a barrier to trade, discriminatory in practice, and contrary to the objective and spirit of GATT. It also conflicts very strongly with section 2 (a) of article 7 of GATT which establishes that value for customs purposes, and I quote:
-should be based on the actual value of the Imported merchandise on which duty Is assessed, or of like merchandise, and should not be based on the value of merchandise of national origin or on arbitrary or fictitious values.

Part (b) of section 2 of article 7 of GATT makes it quite clear, and again I quote:
-actual value should be the price at which, at a time and place determined by the legislation of the country of importation, and in the ordinary course of trade, such or like merchandise is sold or offered for sale under fully competitive conditions.
Therefore, I submit, GATT lays down a natural price in the market of export as the basis for the value for duty and the price is not a guess on the part of the minister or any one else as to what the cost of production may be. All of this, Mr. Speaker, to say that the type of legislation now brought before the house is not compatible with GATT.
In support of my contention I have the great pleasure and honour of citing a person who to my mind is one of the greatest authorities on this matter, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who on December 16, 1953, as reported at page 976 of Hansard of that date, said:
Our interpretation of our obligation under GATT is that we cannot resort to the cost of production price, if there is another way of determining what is the fair market value. It is only when we are prevented from using other ways of determining the fair market value that we feel that under GATT we can resort to investigation of the cost of production.
Later in the same debate, as recorded on the same page of Hansard, Mr. St. Laurent said:
We undertook to allow the importation of goods at the tariff rates based upon fair market value, and this form-
Cost of production. I continue:
-of determining value was discussed in the negotiations and discarded. It was urged that that was not fair market value and that the cost of production might have very little relation to the actual market value of the goods.
Later, as reported at page 977, Mr. St. Laurent said:
Mr. Chairman, it is not the government that the hon. member would have to satisfy that you can go back to the pre-1948 practice and still comply with GATT. It is the other members of GATT. They would regard a return to the 1948 situation as a clear violation of the undertakings of GATT.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that what this legislation is doing is going back to the pre-1948 practice. I also say that as a result of this legislation retaliatory action on the part of other signatories of GATT, provided for under the agreement, could be imposed against Canada and this, of course, would be very prejudicial and have dire consequences on our foreign trade and our general economy in Canada. At a time when there is economic difficulty and unemployment in Canada I submit we cannot afford to risk any further deterioration in our economy by introducing legislation which was so unsuccessful in the past. For these 57071-3-285

That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
this house reaffirms the adherence of Canada to the spirit and objectives of GATT, which are clearly violated in the provisions of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUE FOR DUTY, APPEALS TO EXCHEQUER COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rely, of course, entirely on the citations in Beauchesne and the past rulings of Speakers of this house which are to the effect that when a minister introduces a bill which is an amendment to existing legislation, then it is not open to another member to introduce by way of amendment a proposition which raises a new question and is in that sense not relevant to the bill before the house.
Let us consider the position. Here we have a bill to amend the Customs Act. My hon. friends who have advanced a number of propositions by way of argument as to why that bill, in their opinion, should not be approved on second reading are again, I submit, seeking to put forward now argumentative matter under their amendment that it is not open to them to do. They have advanced a number of propositions which in their view indicate that the bill should not be supported.
But an amendment to the Customs Act, by their own arguments, has nothing to do with GATT whatsoever. They say it is a breach of GATT. We, of course, do not accept that argument but that is a matter of argument. Now, they are leaving the principle of the bill and

advancing an entirely new proposition which is that "this house reaffirm the adherence of Canada to the spirit and objectives of GATT, which are clearly violated in the provisions of this bill." That has nothing to do with the proposal made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) in the legislation before the house. By their very own arguments it has nothing to do with it. Therefore, it is a matter entirely unrelated to it. What they are seeking to do are two things:	one, to advance an argumentative
matter by way of amendment; and, two, to introduce a proposal which has no relation to the subject matter of the resolution before the house.
I recall time after time in my experience when hon. members have sought to introduce new subject matter not related to the principle of a bill and they have been ruled out of order by successive Speakers-I recall Mr. Speaker Macdonald, particularly-on the basis that an amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved. We had just yesterday an example of a proposition which advanced new subject matter which was not relevant, and as I submitted at that time-I recall the point of order was raised by Your Honour-an amendment not relevant could only be introduced after notice. That is the very reason for the provision in the rules that amendments which raise new matter can only be introduced after notice so that the house will not be taken by surprise.
I submit very firmly that this amendment sets forth a proposition which certainly deals with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion, and is shown to be so by the very arguments by the hon. member who has moved the motion and as such it raises a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice. Notice has not been given. I rely on the clear words of subsections 3 and 5 of citation 203 in the point of order which I put forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to have a few words to say on this most interesting and important bill intended by the government, we presume, to prevent unfair competition for certain manufacturers and industries in this country and certain agricultural producers. Before proceeding further, I must say that we think the minister means well so far as this legislation is concerned and we give him full credit for that.
The minister said today that the principle of valuation had been in effect since confederation with modifications from time to time to meet certain conditions and circumstances, but a reading of Hansard and amendments to legislation throughout the years indicate that it has had a zigzag course and the fundamental problem that existed when the Liberals gave effect to dumping legislation in 1922 remains with us today. I remember the 1930 election when the Conservative party campaigned in the fruit districts of the interior of British Columbia and suggested that improvements in dumping legislation would bring stability to the fruit industry, and I am quite sure they intended to do that. They received a very heavy vote in the Okanagan and the Kootenays at that time because of the desire of the fruit growers to find some security so far as their marketing problems were concerned.
But that has not been the result. While I freely admit that this bill is intended to provide some measure of relief to fruit producers and others, the basic problems of these producers-I am speaking now particularly of the fruit industry of which I have some

knowledge-are still with us because we have failed to face them and have relied from time to time on legislation like this. As I read the record, this course of action was commenced by the Liberal government in 1922 and at that time was denounced by the Conservatives. The legislation was then extended and improved under the leadership of Mr. Bennett in 1930 in accordance with his promises to the fruit growers in his campaign of that year. At that time the Liberals opposed Mr. Bennett's amendments to the legislation most vigorously. However, the Liberals continued to support the legislation in principle after their return to office in 1935. Therefore from our point of view we cannot understand how the Liberals can logically oppose or criticize legislation which in principle was begun by them in 1922.

While the type of industry-I mean the manufacturing industry-affected by this bill is generally found in eastern Canada and, as far as western Canada is concerned, in the larger centres, there is included a section in response to the representations of the fruit growing interests in Canada and certain of the vegetable growing interests. On this question I can speak with some experience. I come from a family that came to this country to grow apples and grow rich. I may say that we certainly have not grown rich except in experience. I know all about bringing the virgin forest into production, planting an orchard and working it into shape. We planted a small orchard of about five acres of apples. I remember in the first instance when it cost us $500 an acre to clear the land in the early days. I remember marketing our first box of apples. No one will realize the thrill one gets when

marketing their first box of apples when they are produced from virgin soil. As to the first box of apples we marketed, I was sent by my father to borrow 10 apples from a neighbour in order to make up the box. You can understand what a celebration it was for us with our trying experience, and our experience was the experience of many others.

I mention that only to indicate the hope, labour and capital that went into developing the industry and to indicate that I have some knowledge of the industry in British Columbia from the grass roots up, and that I am very sympathetic indeed to the fruit growers' problems and have a thorough understanding of them.
I also happen to have been a representative of the Kootenays on an organization committee that organized and agitated. That was in a period when respectable Conservatives and Liberals, lay down on the railroad in Kelowna and refused to let the trains move and carried placards around. Actually they acted like members of the working class under similar circumstances. Anyway, we in this group know that, whether they were Conservatives, Liberals or C.C.F., they were in a difficult position. I was on the committee representing the Kootenays that first organized and agitated the fruit growers into action. As a result there was finally placed on the statute books of British Columbia the first marketing legislation which has been a model for the rest of Canada and which the people in Ontario, Quebec and other places have seen fit to follow and to pattern their legislation upon. So, Mr. Speaker, I speak with some interest in and some concern for the welfare of my fellow fruit growers, with a knowledge of production and marketing problems of tree fruit growers in British Columbia.
I know of their efforts to improve production methods, to improve their marketing practices, I realize that they have done practically all that can be done by an intelligent group of growers to organize their production which is on a very excellent basis indeed and to organize their marketing processes. What is required now, both in the federal and in the provincial field, is government action to supplement these self-help efforts that have been going on for the last forty years if the fruit growers not only of British Columbia but of the rest of Canada are going to receive a fair return for their product.
I know that this bill is introduced by the government as an attempt to do something on a temporary basis to meet a very critical situation so far as the fruit industry in British Columbia is concerned. Fruit and vegetables
Customs Act
are very difficult crops to market compared to some other agricultural commodities. You can store beef; you can store grain; and you can store other farm commodities easily; but there are certain fruit crops, such as soft-stone fruits which you cannot store and which must be marketed often under difficult conditions. They are subject to quick and wide price fluctuations due mostly to changes in weather conditions which cause rot or delayed maturity. For instance, a short crop may mature all at once and cause a glut on the market. Bad weather, unseasonable rains, abnormal temperatures, all these things can put a fruit grower in a very difficult position. Crops which affect Canadian producers start in the southern United States and gradually work north. We have that experience every year with respect to certain crops. The early production from such areas usually brings a fair return, which return ensures the producer the over-all cost of production plus some profit in those circumstances. Canadian production commences and must meet competition from the height of the season production from the border states. Certainly our growers seldom enjoy the higher returns they are entitled to from their early production.
We are affected by climate. We are affected by geography and we are affected by the vicissitudes of the fruit industry so far as storage and marketing are concerned. However, conditions respecting a certain group in the producing area in the United States with which they are competing in our market reach the point quite frequently where sales are made at prices which give no return whatsoever to the producer. That is the situation that the government aims to do something towards remedying by the introduction of the particular clause in this bill that deals with fruit. While I recognize that one section of this bill particularly is the government's response to the representations of fruit and vegetable growers, I am sure the majority of them after their experience since the days of the first world war-and I have attended a good many meetings-recognize the fact that it can only be a temporary and a partial remedy to their basic problems and does not provide a comprehensive and long time solution to their marketing problems.
Mr. Speaker, I speak as a free trader in principle. I was brought up in a free trade family. As a matter of fact, my father was a Liberal free trader, my mother was a Conservative free trader and I am a C.C.F. free trader. You can therefore well understand that free trade policies flow through my system. However, regardless of what can be done under this bill, I think if we examine it thoroughly in the light of present world and national conditions, we must recognize that
