the principle of this bill, first of all goes in a direction contrary to the spirit of the times with respect to international markets and the spirit that is being expressed by progressive people in the world who realize that world prosperity depends on an increased flow of goods across international boundaries and so on.
Second, as the previous speaker mentioned, in our opinion, regardless of the best intentions of the government and of the minister, it violates the spirit and the objectives of GATT.
Third, it places potential restrictions on trade with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries. I am sure that an examination of the effect of this bill will indicate that.
Fourth, over a period of time this policy, if carried to its logical conclusion, can invite economic retaliation from the countries directly affected.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, regardless of what the government is trying to do at the present time, I hope that this measure is considered by the government only as a temporary stopgap that will provide time and opportunity for the government to develop a policy in step with the urge and the demand for the extension of international trade as the basis of prosperity for all producers in Canada and all producers in other countries.
As I have said before, this problem of which I am speaking particularly now has been with us since 1922 and in our opinion it will not be solved by the section in this bill that is intended to relieve the situation at this time.
Having expressed our criticism of the bill and our sympathy .for the fruit growers and without questioning in the slightest the motives of the minister, I think we are now called upon to present an alternative policy. If you criticize you must also be prepared to say what you would do if you were in office. I suggest a program along the lines mentioned this morning by the leader of this group, and which I now want to repeat and to mention one or two other aspects relating to the situation which I understand from experience.
We say that we are going to have to tackle the basic problems of these fruit and vegetable growers and I am particularly dealing with that group. It is a funny thing, but I have always noticed at the many conventions I have had the pleasure of attending, both of the fruit growers and of the livestock breeders, that it is very easy to find evidence of the difficulties faced by these people. One can find such an illustration by looking at the physiques of the men attending the conventions. When you attend a livestock convention they are all well padded and of good

weight, whereas those attending the fruit growers' conventions mostly look like me.
We suggest the full use of the agricultural prices stabilization legislation for the establishment of minimum prices. I may say that the stone tree fruit growers or the soft tree fruit growers of British Columbia were very disappointed indeed that the government had failed to recognize in any way their present need by failure to grant any deficiency payments for the 1957 crop. That sort of stabilization is very necessary and I particularly emphasize that this does not apply to apples only but it is also necessary for the stone tree fruit growers because they have to deal with fluctuations in climate, and in marketing conditions caused by geographical conditions, to a greater extent than any other tree fruit growers or, as a matter of fact, any growers of the fruit marketed from this area.
Secondly, we suggest that positive steps be taken to assure adequate and continuous operation and maintenance of processing facilities. I want to say a few words on that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) brings forward his item of $30,000 for the employment of an administrative staff intended to help small business in Canada under present circumstances. We do suggest that both this government and the provincial governments get together with the processors and the canners of this country and get them to recognize their responsibilities to the fruit and vegetable industry across the country and not to allow the continuation of the purchase of the canneries and processing plants in Canada by United States interests and then to have them close them down while the growers in question are in a price squeeze resulting in very little return for their labour.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly at this stage because I believe that is the sense of the house, but I must say I regard this measure as perhaps more important than any which has come before us during this session of parliament. I say that because of its implications in relation to the foreign trade of this country on which so much of our prosperity depends. I will try not to repeat anything in the course of my remarks which has been said already in the speeches which have been made so far and to present in the briefest way possible the arguments I wish to make. I must say that I would wish to speak at greater length on this subject because of my feelings with regard to it, but sensing the feeling of the house I will not do that. I am concerned with the principle of this bill, and I must say this measure has been presented in a strange way to the house because the minister took exactly five minutes on the motion for second reading, three minutes in replying to a proposed amendment and less than one minute in speaking to a point of order.

Customs Act
In speaking to that point of order he raised a question as to what was the principle of the bill. I had assumed until that time that this was anti-dumping legislation, legislation aimed at preventing the trade practice commonly known as dumping, a term which is probably ill-defined but which is well understood by everyone concerned with trade. In any event I want to point out that the principle of a bill can only be determined through a study of what is actually included in the bill. In this particular measure there are five clauses. Clause No. 1 repeals sections 35 to 40 of the Customs Act and substitutes new clauses in their place. The new clauses which it is proposed to substitute begin with clause 35 which reads:
(1) The value for duty of goods imported shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 36 to 40B.
And so on. The next new clause to be substituted is clause 36 which begins:
Subject to section 38, the value for duty shall, notwithstanding any invoice or affidavit to the contrary-
And so on.
The next new clause to be substituted is clause 37 and it goes on to say:
Subject to section 38, where like goods were not sold for home consumption, or were not sold for home consumption in the circumstances described in section 36, but similar goods were so sold, the value for duty shall-
And so on. That is the subject matter of that particular clause. The new proposed clause 38 starts off this way:
Where in any case or class of cases.. .the value for duty cannot be determined . . . the value for duty shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes.
I will only read a sentence of clause 39 to illustrate my point. It says:
Where the minister is satisfied that material injury has been or may be caused to any industry in Canada or any portion thereof.. .the governor in council may order that the value for duty of those goods or that class of goods shall be increased-
And so on.
The proposed new clause 40 reads:
Where sufficient information has not been furnished or is not available to enable the determination of cost of production, gross profit or fair market value under section 36, 37 or 39, the cost of production, gross profit or fair market value, as the case may be, shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes.
Then the proposed new clause 40A goes on to set out the whole procedure with regard to valuation and uses the expression, beginning at line 29:
The value for duty shall be the amount for which the goods were sold, less the amount, if any, by which the fair market value of the goods has decreased between the time of purchase and the time of exportation.
[Mr. Mcllraith.j
We could go through every subclause and find a similar reference to value for duty. The proposed new clause 40B begins:
If the value for duty as determined under sections 36 to 40A does not include-
And so on. Clause 2 of the bill deals with section 45 of the act. It repeals that section and substitutes a new one. This procedural clause reads as follows:
Any of the parties to an appeal under section 44-
Section 44 is not dealt with in the bill, but it starts off this way:
A person who deems himself aggrieved by a decision of the deputy minister
(a) as to tariff classification or value for duty.
Clause 3 of the bill substitutes a new section 46(1) and this again deals with valuation or tariff classification. Note the term "valuation." And then 46A makes reference specifically to sections 43, 44 and 45 of the act, all of which refer to valuation for duty.
Clause 4 of the bill now before us deals with invoices and the fair market value of goods determined in accordance with sections 36 to 40B, every one of which sections refers to value for duty.
Now we come to clause 5 of the bill. Clause 5 refers to paragraph (b) of subsection (7) of section 40A of the act. It will be found that that also brings in the question of value in paragraph 5 which is concerned with the proclamation of the governor in council.
What I want to point out is that every clause in this bill deals with the matter of value for duty of goods being imported into this country and that every proposed new section of the act deals with that subject. From this we can arrive at only one conclusion: notwithstanding the argument of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), which he made in the course of a discussion on a point of order, that this does not deal with value for duty, it does, and it deals with nothing else.
That is the whole principle of the bill. I do not think the minister should deal with it other than on that basis.
After recognizing the bill as being an antidumping measure, a measure providing means for fixing the value for duty purposes, I wish to place on the record two clauses of the GATT agreement, clause 2 (a) and 2 (b) of article 7, which read as follows:
2. (a) The value for customs purposes of imported merchandise should be based on the actual value of the imported merchandise on which duty is assessed, or of like merchandise, and should not be based on the value of merchandise of national origin or on arbitrary or fictitious values.
(b) "Actual value" should be the price at which, at a time and place determined by the legislation of the country of importation, and in the ordinary course of trade, such or like merchandise is sold or offered for sale under fully competitive conditions. To the extent to which the price of such

or like merchandise is governed by the quantity in a particular transaction, the price to be considered should uniformly be related to either (i) comparable quantities, or (ii) quantities not less favourable to importers than those in which the greater volume of the merchandise is sold in the trade between the countries of exportation and importation.
I could go on reading other clauses from the GATT agreement to illustrate my point but perhaps these are sufficient for that purpose to the extent to which they deal with value for duty.
That brings me to this point. As indicated in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in the early stages of the debate on this bill, this measure is one in which the government is asking added powers for the executive to fix value for duty purposes. It is requesting extraordinary additional powers. I will not develop that argument further because an amendment was advanced on that point which has been disposed of by the house. As indicated by the vote the house wants to proceed with the bill notwithstanding the points outlined by my leader. I shall not reopen the argument in that respect.
The minister has made no case for seeking these extraordinary powers. He has not argued nor illustrated the inadequacies of the existing legislation. He made no case on that point whatsoever. The measure before us does not simply deal with changes in the existing legislation but it extends the right of the executive to fix values in the way indicated in the argument presented by my leader this morning. The effect of granting these powers is going to injure our trade. I ask hon. members to bear in mind what I said about the government having put forward no case whatever concerning why the executive should be granted these additional arbitrary powers. My fear is that Canada's trade will suffer. Canadian trade sharply increased since 1946. Perhaps it is unnecessary to place on the record all the figures I have before me relating to this point. I shall put only the total exports on the record. In 1946 Canada's total exports amounted to $2,339 million and in 1957 they amounted to $4,934 million.
That vast trade was built up by this country with a great number of other nations. It was built up at a time when efforts were being made to free and increase trade all over the world. One of those efforts was the general agreement on tariff and trade to which we should adhere. That may come as news to some hon. members of this house but I do not want to argue that point. Nevertheless, that is how the trade was built up. We are now being asked to jeopardize our relations with all the foreign countries with

whom we trade. We are now putting them in the position where they could argue that we have violated the agreement to which we are a signatory. Why? No reason has been given to us by the government and we are entitled to have reasons given. If there is a fear of the evil of dumping then the house should be told about it. This is a drastic and serious remedy we are seeking; but a remedy against what? Nothing. There is no evidence of the inadequacy of the existing legislation or, if there is, it has not been put on the record.
I feel that something should be said in reply to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) and I shall reply very briefly. The hon. member tried to indicate that this bill would help labour. This bill is the very antithesis of help to labour. It is the very thing that will increase unemployment in this country and unemployment is a worrisome problem to many Canadians at this time. I want to remind the hon. gentleman that the method of determining value for duty incorporated in part in the bill now before the house is the method that was brought into the house and enacted into legislation by a Conservative government headed by the late Lord Bennett, in the 1930's. If the hon. member will look at Canadian trade statistics he will observe what happened to Canada's trade under that type of legislation. If he studies the problem he will see the severity with which dumping legislation was administered at that time. It undoubtedly contributed to tensions in international trade and to the reduction of trade.
When the hon. member talks about pay for labour let me remind him that coming from Rosthern he knows what the term "Bennett buggy" means. He also knows what hon. members of this house are talking about when they refer to the time when labour in this country got 20 cents a day. He understands those references.

Have you ever seen an amendment before which says that the house declines to proceed with a bill? It is a sheer negative to express reasons possibly to show that the house declines to proceed with a bill the fundamental terms of which are repugnant. I suggest in the first place the form of the amendment is completely out of order.
In so far as the bill itself is concerned, Your Honour said you were somewhat troubled by my reference to the division of legislative powers contained within the bill. What the hon. member for Ottawa West said, of course, is perfectly right. Certain subsections here deal with valuing procedures. I point out to Your Honour that this bill contains only three sections.

speechtext:
Absolutely, only one section deals with valuation procedure. We turn to section 3. Section 1, of course, is something which provides for repealing sections 35 to 40 of the Customs Act, and we go on to various subsections set forth there. Then, we come to section 3 which gives power to

the deputy minister to refer any question to the tariff board. That deals with appeal procedures. That has nothing whatever to do with GATT or anything of the kind. Then, the next section has to do with importation of goods. Any seditious material comes under section 3, and section 4 is also a matter having no reference whatsoever to valuations. Your Honour is in this position. One out of the four sections of this bill deals with valuation procedure. The Leader of the Opposition shakes his head, but that is correct. It is true that section 1 sets forth five old sections or new sections of a bill.
In so far as this bill is concerned, that is the situation. I want to emphasize this, Mr. Speaker. Of those five sections only one is new; only one can be construed as a violation of GATT, section 39, and when we come to 39, either tonight or tomorrow, we will be perfectly prepared to argue with those who wish to argue whether 39 is a violation of GATT or not. All of the other subsections, except subsection 39, are simply administrative practices which have been carried on under government administration and all that they do is to clarify the matter. There is no change in principle whatsoever.
There is no point in extending the argument on this, Mr. Speaker. You can make your ruling and it, of course, will be dealt with and we will deal with the amendment as Your Honour sees fit to rule, but I do say very strenuously that this bill does not in itself constitute a violation of GATT. It has three different parts, but the main part is the longer part, consisting of four or five pages. There is only one subsection in that which could possibly be construed as an amendment of GATT and that can be argued, I submit to Your Honour, when the section is dealt with in the committee and not before. Surely the bill should not be ruled out of order, or the house decline to proceed with it, because one subsection of the many may or may not be a violation of GATT.

Mr. Speaker, I have been out looking up some of the previous occasions on which amendments have been ruled out of order on the grounds either that they raised new matter which could only be raised after notice or else that they were irrelevant to the terms of the bill. I have not Hansard before me; the volumes are coming in, but on second reading of a bill the principle is established most clearly that any amendment must be strictly relevant to the principle of a bill.
This is a bill to amend the Customs Act. My hon. friends have sought twice now to move an amendment which alleges that the bill is contrary to the spirit and objectives of GATT. That, Mr. Speaker, is a matter of argument that may be in order but as an amendment it is not relevant to the principle of the bill. Your Honour has already ruled out of order the last amendment which read:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house reaffirms the adherence of Canada to the spirit and objectives of GATT, which are clearly violated in provisions of this bill."
As I say, this is a matter of argument which may be in order but as a matter of amendment it is not relevant to the principle of the bill. Now they are trying to do the same thing by alleging that:
This house declines to proceed with a bill the fundamental terms of which are repugnant to the spirit and objectives of the treaty obligations of Canada under GATT.
There are a number of occasions, and especially in the parliament from 1949 to 1953, where Mr. Speaker Macdonald ruled that on all occasions amendments with respect to the principle of motions or bills must be strictly relevant. He dealt with the argument put forward by my hon. friends opposite that the amendment might advance a proposition which, as they say, asserts a principle different from or opposed to the principle of the bill. In every case Mr. Speaker Macdonald ruled that while that is a principle of amendment nevertheless the amendment must be so phrased that it is strictly relevant to the principle of the bill itself.
I have not had much time since returning from the library to find the most apt amendment. I have four occasions here before me and perhaps I might refer Your Honour to them. There is October 17, 1949, pages 856 and 857; April 21, 1952, pages 1438 and 1439.

That is on all fours with the argument they are putting forward tonight that the treaty obligations of Canada under GATT are relevant to the principles of this bill. The one is just as relevant as the other. Mr. Speaker Macdonald dealt at length with that point. He said that it was indeed in accordance with citation 657 of Beauchesne's third edition. He said that it was competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill to move as an amendment to the question a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to or differing from the principles, policy or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction or prosecution or otherwise opposed to its project.
But he went on to say that he would refer hon. members to citation 354 of Beauchesne's third edition which reads as follows:
An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.

There are other occasions both with respect to bills and resolutions. Another occasion I have before me was on November 23, 1949, when there was a motion before the house for the second reading of a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act. Once again the amendment moved on that occasion by the present Prime Minister, who was then the member for Lake Centre, set forth a different proposition, suggested that the bill should not now be read a second time but that certain different courses should be followed. In this case the amendment was as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"While this house is at all times anxious to assist in remedying any defects in the law with respect to combinations in restraint of trade that operate against the public interest, it regrets that His Majesty's ministers have failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of publication of reports under the Combines Investigation Act and that before inviting parliament to enact the said bill have failed to give any assurance that there will be no similar breach of the constitution in respect of this or any other act passed by the parliament of Canada."
Here, Mr. Speaker, was an amendment which dealt with the conduct of the government with respect to the requirements of the Combines Investigation Act which was then being amended by the bill before the house. Mr. Speaker Macdonald ruled that the amendment raised a matter which was different from the principle advanced in the motion before the house, that it was not relevant and was therefore not in order. I submit that what the opposition is trying to do here is exactly on all fours with that occasion. They are in effect condemning the government for introducing a bill, as they allege, which is repugnant to the spirit and objectives of GATT. In other words, they are expressing an opinion on this bill in relation to GATT in exactly the same way as the hon. member for Lake Centre, as he then was, introduced an amendment expressing an opinion with regard to the government's actions under the Combines Investigation Act but with relation to a different subject. Yet on that occasion the Speaker ruled that the amendment was

not relevant and could not be introduced notwithstanding the provisions of citation 657 of Beauchesne's third edition.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that if Your Honour will look at the whole trend of decisions, particularly during the parliament from 1949 to 1953 and also in the parliament from 1953 to 1957 and earlier parliaments, Your Honour will find that the trend of the rulings has been that amendments introduced may not raise a matter which should really only be raised after notice because otherwise the house would be taken by surprise, and the rule that requires that all matters of debate must have proper notice would be set at naught.
My hon. friends are introducing an amendment here which seeks not to debate the merits of the principle of the bill before the house but to debate the merits of the GATT treaty. I submit to you, sir, on that ground that in general such amendments are out of order. I also submit that it is out of order on the same grounds that you ruled the previous amendment out of order, namely, that these are matters which may be made the subject of amendment in committee; that any specific provision which can be shown in committee to violate any particular of Canada's treaty obligations can be made the subject of an amendment in committee. What my hon. friends are seeking to do here is in particular to anticipate a discussion which should be raised in committee on the clauses.

If no other hon. members wish to speak, I will give my decision. This is the third time I have had to deal with this matter today. I will not repeat what was said previously. The first question which must be considered is relevancy. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), in acknowledging that it would be relevant to debate whether the sections of this bill are in conflict with our obligations under GATT, thereby acknowledges that an amendment directed to that same purpose is relevant, because if it is relevant to debate it,-if the amendment is otherwise good-it is relevant to move an amendment declaratory of a principle to the same effect.
I am troubled by the minister's statement that this is an argument. It is an argument; any assertion of principle would be an argument. Hence I do not think the issue should be determined on that ground at all.
Then the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) rather underplays the importance of the value for duty part of this bill. In what he said I think he in effect acknowledged that it is the one substantial change in the bill.

Many changes are made but they are more or less procedural changes. They are not important changes until you come to section 39 which is new and which is an important change. The other items are procedural. It therefore seems to me that the value for duty strikes at the basic principle of the bill. On that ground I do not think that the principle of the amendment should be deferred for consideration in committee.
It remains then to consider whether this amendment is different from the one that I
Customs Act
ruled out earlier. The earlier amendment called on the house to adhere to its GATT obligations, and opened the door to a very extended debate which might have nothing at all to do with this bill. This amendment calls on the house to refuse to read this bill the second time because its terms are repugnant to the spirit and objectives of the treaty obligations of Canada under GATT, thereby declaring a principle which is to my mind relevant and which is adverse to the principle of the bill. The amendment certainly is opposed to the terms of the bill in that it calls on the house to decline to proceed. To my mind it is not a mere direct negative. It meets all these tests. It seems to me that on second reading, where the house has the acknowledged right to debate the principles which are involved in the bill, it is preferable not to be too restrictive in the type of amendment which brings before the house in specific form and emphasizes the principles which are involved, the principle in this case being that the sections of this bill may be adverse to the spirit and objectives of the treaty obligations of Canada under GATT. I therefore rule the amendment to be in order and I shall now put the question.
